text:
A Trump-appointed federal judge on Monday tossed out a Department of Justice lawsuit that aimed to invalidate state and local “sanctuary” policies, which limit information-sharing and cooperation between local law enforcement agencies and immigration enforcement.

The lawsuit, filed in September, was one of at least 27 such cases filed against more than 20 cities, counties and states during the first year of President Donald Trump’s second term. It preceded Operation Metro Surge, during which thousands of immigration agents arrested thousands of immigrants; shot three people, killing two; and sparked major protests.

Leaders at the Department of Homeland Security repeatedly pointed to state and local governments’ refusal to assist in immigration enforcement as a reason for not ending the operation sooner.

In its complaint, the DOJ challenged several state and local policies: a Minnesota law preventing the state Department of Driver and Vehicle Services from sharing data with immigration agencies; Minneapolis and St. Paul policies barring local police from enforcing immigration laws; an attorney general’s legal advisory prohibiting Minnesota law enforcement agencies from holding someone based on a request from federal immigration authorities if the person would otherwise be released from custody; and a Hennepin County policy modeled on that attorney general’s advisory.

Eric C. Tostrud, chief judge for the District of Minnesota, dismissed all of the claims. He primarily cited the Tenth Amendment’s anticommandeering doctrine, which prohibits the federal government from forcing state and local authorities to carry out tasks — such as immigration enforcement — which are the sole responsibility of the federal government.

text:
A federal judge has ordered immigration officials to release a 32-year-old Florida resident from custody after she spent the last ten days in the U.S. Immigration of Customs Enforcement field office near the Burlington Mall.

Maria Rosales was arrested on July 10 at Logan Airport after coming to town for a Noah Kahan concert, and held in the controversial facility while her lawyers argued for her release.

In a sworn affidavit obtained by WBUR, Rosales detailed "tough" and "uncomfortable" conditions similar to those reported over the last year by other Burlington detainees, and which have drawn scrutiny from members of Congress and the public.

"We have to beg for water ... We've been in the same clothes for weeks ... The room is extremely hot with all those bodies in a tiny cell ... The food is inedible," she wrote in the affidavit. "Some of the girls here refuse to eat because the food is vile and they couldn't stomach it."

Rosales said she didn't always have access to a shower, and that her request for Tylenol while she was on her period was "disregarded."

She also wrote that she and other detainees "have to beg for phone time to speak to our lawyers and family," and that one day, "the officers got angry and claimed the phones were down all day."

Rosales was born in Colombia and came to the U.S. with her parents when she was 4-years-old, her lawyer Todd Pomerleau said in an interview. She grew up in Florida, he said, and leads a performing arts nonprofit for youth. Her affidavit said she is studying at Miami Dade College to be a nurse.

She has had legal status in the U.S. under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, or DACA, which was established under former President Barack Obama to give temporary status and work authorization to undocumented immigrants brought to the country as children.

According to Pomerleau, Rosales applied to renew her DACA status three years ago and her case is pending. So she was surprised when ICE agents stopped her at Logan. They told her she had a deportation order from 2017 — the same year she’d originally applied for DACA — and had allegedly missed a court date. According to her affidavit, she was not presented with an arrest warrant at Logan.

Pomerleau suspects the ordeal stems from an incident in 2017 when Rosales and her family were briefly stopped at a border checkpoint while driving across the country.

"I believe I am a worthy member of society," she wrote in her affidavit. "I was unaware I had an order of deportation in 2017. If I knew I had a court date, I would have attended."

As WBUR has previously reported, the field office was not designed to be a long-term holding center; it's an intake center, where immigrants arrested by ICE are brought for booking before being moved to longer-term detention centers.

But beginning sometime in the spring of 2025, as the Trump administration launched a major immigration effort in Massachusetts, many arrested by ICE found themselves stuck in the building's small concrete holding cells for days — and sometimes weeks.

Some, like Milford high school student Marcelo Gomes da Silva, have said they were held with dozens of other people in a single room. Others said they weren't given access to showers or sanitary supplies. And many described sleeping on concrete floors with just a mylar blanket.

"These claims that there are subprime conditions or overcrowding are false," a spokesperson for ICE said in an email. "The ICE Burlington facility has an abundance of supplies, including food, assorted snacks, water, personal hygiene, and bedding materials."

A federal court ruling in June said ICE would have to seek permission to hold people for more than 12 hours at an administrative office like the one in Burlington. The ICE spokesperson did not say if the agency had obtained that permission here.

Pomerleau said he’s heard similar complaints about the conditions in Burlington from several other clients over the last year, including some of the women arrested at an Allston carwash last November.

"They were held there, six to 10 days," he said. "One of them they were feeding donuts to was a diabetic,” and her blood sugar had spiked by the time she was released.

The day after Rosales was arrested and brought to the Burlington ICE office, her lawyer filed what's known as a habeas petition in federal court to challenge her detention and prevent the government from transferring her out of Massachusetts. A judge granted the petition the same day.

The federal government filed its response July 16, claiming Rosales was still eligible for deportation, Pomerleau said.

"They claim pending DACA renewal doesn’t prevent deportation," he said. "We strongly disagreee."

On Monday, the judge seemed to agree. He ordered ICE to release Rosales by 7 p.m. and said she could not be re-arrested "absent compliance with the applicable statutory and regulatory procedures."

Pomerleau said his colleagues attempted to visit Rosales in Burlington this past Friday, but were initially denied entrance. They were eventually allowed in to speak with her, though immigration officials brought them all to a private conference room, so they did not see the space where she was being held.

"She said it's the worst treatment she's had in her life. She's begging for water, sanitary supplies," Pomerleau said. "It just seems like there's all these health code violations."

Since last year, when accounts of conditions at the Burlington facility first began to surface, local officials have sought access for building department staff to inspect it for zoning or health violations. A judge denied the town's request for a court order last fall, in part because she said the detainee accounts presented as evidence in the case were too old.

Rosales' case could present a new opening for town officials.

"We are aware of what has happened to Ms. Rosales and it’s as distressing as all of the stories and accounts we have heard coming from 1000 District Ave.," said Burlington select board member Mike Espejo. "Our goal to get our building inspector in there has not changed and we will continue to try and accomplish that through all available legal channels."

description:
Two U.S. Catholic bishops are lamenting recent deadly immigration enforcement encounters, calling for God-given human dignity to be respected in every individual.
On July 14, ICE agents shot and killed 26-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian, after being stopped by ICE agents near a laundromat.
The Trump administration briefly halted, then resumed, ICE traffic stops in the wake of the deaths.
"Our pastoral concerns are distinct from what the civil law itself may permit," said the two bishops.
In a report released in June, Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights counted 52 deaths in ICE custody during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration.
text:
Two U.S. Catholic bishops are lamenting recent deadly immigration enforcement encounters, calling for God-given human dignity to be respected in every individual.

"As Catholics, we believe that all persons are created in the image and likeness of God and, therefore, grieve all situations where human life is brought to an unnatural end. This is a core teaching of our faith and one we can never grow weary of proclaiming as disciples of Our Lord Jesus Christ," said Bishop Daniel E. Garcia of Austin, Texas, and Bishop Brendan J. Cahill of Victoria, Texas.

The two issued a July 20 joint pastoral reflection as chairs, respectively, of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' Subcommittee for the Promotion of Racial Justice and Reconciliation and the USCCB's Committee on Migration.

Their statement follows three separate deaths recorded days apart in July amid operations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers as they implement the Trump administration's hardline crackdown on immigration.

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Houston area man, was fatally shot en route to work in his vehicle July 7 during an ICE traffic stop. On July 14, ICE agents shot and killed 26-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian, after being stopped by ICE agents near a laundromat. Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, a 28-year-old man from Mexico, was struck and killed by a tractor trailer July 15 in St. Augustine, Florida, while fleeing ICE and Homeland Security agents on foot.

ICE's claims that Salgado and Durán attempted to ram officials with their respective vehicles have been disputed, with Houston law enforcement officials expressing frustration over the federal agency's lack of collaboration in investigating forensic evidence in Salgado's death.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed that Salgado — a Mexican national who had been in the U.S. for some 35 years, and who was in the process of obtaining legal authorization to reside and work in the country — was not the intended target of the ICE operation in which he died.

In Colorado, an employee of the GEO Group — a private firm that contracts with ICE to operate its Aurora processing center — opened fire July 16 on a protester at the site, injuring the woman's foot.

The Trump administration briefly halted, then resumed, ICE traffic stops in the wake of the deaths.

In their statement, Bishops Garcia and Cahill quoted from the USCCB's November 2025 special pastoral message on immigration: "We are disturbed when we see among our people a climate of fear and anxiety around questions of profiling and immigration enforcement."

Drawing on the USCCB's 2018 pastoral letter on racism, "Open Wide Our Hearts," the bishops stressed that "racial profiling in particular violates God-given dignity," adding the practice "also inflicts profound harm on individuals, families, and communities by fostering fear, eroding trust, and increasing the risk of unjust and even tragic outcomes. "

"Our pastoral concerns are distinct from what the civil law itself may permit," said the two bishops.

They warned that "acts that diminish or disregard the dignity of any person or group of people should never be normalized in our society," pointing to both "the dehumanization of immigrants, regardless of their legal status" and "the vilification of law enforcement officers" as examples.

Bishops Garcia and Cahill said they "continue to affirm the legitimate role of civil authorities to implement the law in a humane manner and with respect for fundamental human rights, including the rights to life and due process."

Underscoring that "the power of the state must always be exercised within the limits of the moral law," they called for "accountability, transparency, and justice, which require that meaningful reforms be made to our immigration system."

The bishops said they "join in praying for the souls of those killed and for their families, for our nation, and for all those entrusted with the duties of public service."

They also prayed "for an end to dehumanizing rhetoric, racial prejudice, and violence and for a renewed commitment to recognizing the inherent dignity of every person as a child of God," and pleaded for "the intercession of Mary, Our Mother, who is the model of perfect faith in times of grief, hardship, and uncertainty."

According to data analyzed by The Guardian, eight persons — including U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti — have been shot to death by federal immigration agents under the current Trump administration as of July 15, with 13 injured and another 9 other shooting incidents with no injuries.

In a report released in June, Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights counted 52 deaths in ICE custody during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration. The two organizations said ICE "fails to disclose adequate information about the circumstances surrounding deaths in its custody," with medical neglect suspected as a key factor.

As of April, more than 60,000 are in ICE custody, the majority of whom (just under 71%) have no criminal convictions, according to Syracuse University's Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.

text:
With this complaint Khalil sought $20 million – or an official apology and an end to unconstitutional policy

July 20, 2026, New York – Mahmoud Khalil filed his second federal lawsuit in a week today. The latest case, against the Trump administration, seeks accountability for his wrongful arrest, wrongful detention, and other abuses. It comes on the heels of a separate lawsuit in which he sued individual members of the administration, including Stephen Miller and Marco Rubio, and three anti-Palestinian organizations – Canary Mission, Betar, and the Heritage Foundation – for conspiring to deprive him of his constitutional rights. Both filed by the Center for Constitutional Rights, the suits reflect Mr. Khalil’s resolve to push back against his persecutors 16 months into an ordeal that began when federal agents abducted him in March 2025 in retaliation for his advocacy for Palestinian rights and detained him for 104 days, forcing him to miss the birth of his first child.

For this type of lawsuit, Mr. Khalil was first required to file an administrative claim with the government; after the agencies denied the complaint and failed to address the harms it raised, he was then able to file a federal lawsuit, which he did today. His original claim was filed on July 10, 2025, and asked for $20 million in damages that he would use to help others similarly targeted by the Trump administration and Columbia University; in the claim, he said he would accept, in lieu of payment, an official apology and abandonment of the administration’s unconstitutional policy.

“Not only is the U.S. government using taxpayer dollars to fund Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza, but they are weaponizing the immigration and legal systems to target those who speak out against them,” said Mr. Khalil. “There has to be accountability for political retaliation and abuse of power. With these lawsuits, I am pursuing justice against everyone who contributed to my unlawful detention and spread lies in an attempt to destroy my reputation. I’m holding the U.S. government accountable not just for myself, but for everyone they try to silence through intimidation, detention, or deportation.”

Malice marked the treatment of Mr. Khalil from the outset, as the administration sought to terrorize him and his family. Today’s suit cites a range of abuses, including false arrest, false imprisonment, abuse of the legal system, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. Mr. Khalil brings the case under the Federal Tort Claims Act, a 1946 statute that allows individuals to sue the U.S. government for civil law violations. He is seeking damages directly from the United States for torts, or wrongs, committed by officers of the State Department, the Department of Homeland Security, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement. His conspiracy case, filed last Tuesday and brought under the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, differs in that it names as defendants administration officials in their individual capacities and the private actors they conspired with.

“Mr. Khalil will never get back the months stolen from him when he was abducted and unlawfully held in immigration detention, leading him to miss his child’s birth and first months of life,” said Samah Sisay, a staff attorney at the Center for Constitutional Rights. “The Trump administration must take responsibility for its unconstitutional targeting of Mr. Khalil and compensate him for the severe harms that he continues to navigate due to its unlawful actions.”

Mr. Khalil was the first victim in a series of wrongful arrests of Palestinian rights advocates – a campaign by the administration to weaken the Palestinian solidarity movement and punish those who spoke out against Israel’s U.S.-enabled genocide in Gaza.

Mr. Khalil’s immigration and habeas cases are ongoing.

title: Immigration – Habeas corpus – Transfer - Massachusetts Lawyers Weekly
description:
Where a petitioner has requested habeas corpus relief, a transfer to the Southern District of Mississippi, where the petitioner is now confined, is appropriate.
“On June 23, 2026, [the petitioner] was arrested by ICE near the Massachusetts–New Hampshire border while on his way to work.
… Following his arrest, he was detained at the Plymouth County Correctional Facility (‘PCCF’) in Massachusetts, where he remained for a week.
… “In their answer filed July 8, the respondents argued that this Court never acquired habeas jurisdiction over [the] petition, as he had left Massachusetts hours before its filing.
“Accordingly, it is hereby ordered that this action shall be transferred to the United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi.” Macas Gutama v. Moniz et al.
text:
Where a petitioner has requested habeas corpus relief, a transfer to the Southern District of Mississippi, where the petitioner is now confined, is appropriate.

“On June 23, 2026, [the petitioner] was arrested by ICE near the Massachusetts–New Hampshire border while on his way to work. … Following his arrest, he was detained at the Plymouth County Correctional Facility (‘PCCF’) in Massachusetts, where he remained for a week. …

“Pursuant to this Court’s standard practice in matters such as this one, the Court promptly issued an order directing the Clerk to serve the petition and prohibiting the respondents from removing [the petitioner] from Massachusetts or the United States without advance written notice. … The same order required the respondents to ‘file a notice in writing on the docket in this action stating the name and location of the facility in which Petitioner is confined’ if they disputed the allegation that he ‘is presently confined in the District of Massachusetts.’ … Per that requirement, the respondents filed a notice early the next morning (July 1, 2026, at 6:39 AM) informing the Court that [the petitioner] was detained at a facility in Natchez, Mississippi, having departed on a flight from Bedford, Massachusetts, at 2:11 PM on June 30 — more than two hours before the petition was filed. …

“In their answer filed July 8, the respondents argued that this Court never acquired habeas jurisdiction over [the] petition, as he had left Massachusetts hours before its filing. …

“In support of his plea that this Court acquired and should exercise jurisdiction, [the petitioner] relies on an exception to the generally applicable district-of-confinement rule. … But the ‘narrow’ exception he invokes applies only when a case presents ‘extraordinary circumstances,’ such as where ICE has ‘spirited’ a detainee ‘from one site to another in an attempt to manipulate jurisdiction.’ … Here, as in Vasquez [v. Reno, 233 F.3d 688 (1st Cir. 2000)] (and unlike in Suri [v. Trump, 785 F. Supp. 3d 128 (E.D. Va. 2025]), [the petitioner] ‘has neither marshaled facts suggesting furtiveness nor made a showing of … bad faith.’ …

“The record before the Court establishes that [the petitioner] was held in Massachusetts, at PCCF, for seven days before his transfer to Mississippi. This fact alone substantially undermines his characterization of his transfer as so ‘hasty’ and ‘fast’ as to have been ‘arbitrary and capricious.’ …

“In light of the foregoing, the Court finds [the petitioner] has not established that this is a case warranting an exception to the generally applicable rules concerning habeas jurisdiction. The Court concludes that it lacks jurisdiction in these circumstances. Transfer of this action to the district in which [the petitioner] is presently confined — where he was headed by plane when the petition was filed, and where he arrived hours after its filing — is appropriate.

“Accordingly, it is hereby ordered that this action shall be transferred to the United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi.”

Macas Gutama v. Moniz et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 02-352-26) (6 pages) (Sorokin, J.) (Civil No. 26-13016-LTS) (July 14, 2026).

text:
Where a plaintiff has challenged the defendants’ termination of his Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) record, the plaintiff’s complaint was not rendered moot by virtue of the defendants’ reactivation of the plaintiff’s SEVIS record, but the plaintiff’s complaint should be dismissed to the extent that he seeks enjoinment of “further adverse action based on the terminated SEVIS record unless due process is provided.”

Accordingly, the defendants’ motion to dismiss is allowed in part and denied in part.

“Defendants contend that, because [the plaintiff]’s SEVIS record has been reinstated retroactive to the date of termination, there are no longer grounds upon which this court may grant relief. …

“As set forth below, the court joins several other district courts in finding that, under the voluntary cessation doctrine, [the plaintiff]’s Complaint [Doc. No. 1] was not rendered moot by virtue of Defendants’ reactivation of [the plaintiff]’s SEVIS record. …

“Resolving all inferences in [the plaintiff]’s favor, as the court must do at this stage, the court finds that Defendants’ reactivation of the SEVIS records is akin to the kind of ‘opportunism, on the part of the defendant, that typically supports invocations of mootness exceptions where voluntary cessation of the challenged conduct is at issue.’ …

As to the second condition, Defendants have failed to carry their burden of demonstrating ‘that it is absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.’ …

“Accordingly, the court concludes that [the plaintiff]’s Complaint [Doc. No. 1] has not been rendered moot by the reactivation of his SEVIS record in April 2025. …

“To the extent [the plaintiff] seeks enjoinment of unspecified ‘collateral reputational and administrative harm,’ including unidentified ‘potential future adverse treatment by DHS, ICE, CBP, or [DOS] based on the erroneous data’ leading to the April 2025 SEVIS record termination, … the court finds that [the plaintiff] has not sufficiently demonstrated that these future harms are ‘certainly impending’ or are at a ‘substantial’ risk of occurring. … Stated differently, the ‘collateral, reputational, and administrative harm’ [the plaintiff] asserts constitute a ‘hypothetical future injury’ that ‘does not give [him] standing’ to seek remediation in this manner. …

“For the foregoing reasons, Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss [Doc. No. 25] is granted in part and denied in part:

“1. The Motion [Doc. No. 25] is denied insofar as Defendants seek dismissal of the Complaint [Doc. No. 1] in its entirety for mootness.

“2. The Motion [Doc. No. 25] is granted insofar as Defendants seek dismissal of so much of the Complaint [Doc. No. 1] that seeks enjoinment of ‘further adverse action based on the terminated SEVIS record unless due process is provided.’ …”

Raj v. United States Department of Homeland Security, et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 02-349-26) (14 pages) (Talwani, J.) (Civil Action No. 1:25-cv-10911-IT) (July 13, 2026).

text:
A sheriff’s lawsuit challenging a state law that prohibits local law enforcement officers from working with federal immigration authorities was tossed out by a federal judge.

Attorney General Phil Weiser last summer sued a Mesa County sheriff’s deputy after he tipped off immigration officials about a Utah college student he had just pulled over on a traffic violation.

The Mesa deputy, Alexander Zwinck, was accused of informing Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers about Caroline Dias Goncalves, who was traveling on Interstate 70. Zwinck gave her a warning on an alleged traffic violation, but then told immigration officials that she could be in the country without documentation and they stopped her a few miles down the road without a warrant.

Dias Goncalves, who was a 19-year-old nursing student, had no criminal record, but was detained for more than two weeks. She came to the United States from Brazil with her parents as a 7-year-old. She is out of custody now and is party to a larger class action lawsuit filed by the American Civil Liberties Union against the federal government about warrantless ICE arrests.

Weiser, at the time, filed an unusual lawsuit against Deputy Zwinck, asserting he had no right to share, or even look into, Dias Goncalves’ personal identifying information for purposes of assisting ICE. The attorney general filed the suit under a 6-year-old Colorado law that allows law enforcement officers to be sued for misconduct.

Then, Mesa County Sheriff Todd Rowell, Undersheriff Matthew King and Capt. Curtis Brammer, who supervised Zwinck, countersued the state on grounds that the state law banning local law enforcement from working with ICE is both vague and violates the Supremacy Clause of the United States Constitution, which establishes that federal law is the supreme law of the land.

In a ruling issued Friday, U.S. District Court Judge Gordon Gallagher disagreed.

Gallagher wrote that the sheriff and his deputies lack standing to bring suit against the state. The federal judge argued that Zwinck’s conduct falls squarely within the wording of the state statute.

The state law “only applies to intentional sharing of information for federal immigration purposes, and the text unambiguously attaches liability to the intention of the individual sharing information, not the individual or entity receiving information,” the judge wrote, bolding the word in his ruling.

The original case against Zwinck was dropped by Weiser after the deputy chose to leave his job as a Mesa County Sheriff’s Office. He said he was leaving Colorado law enforcement, according to a resignation letter.

The Mesa County Sheriff’s Office said in an email that they’ll use the ruling to guide training and operations and comply with Colorado law.

“I appreciate the time and attention Judge Gallagher gave this case,” Rowell said in a statement. “It is essential for local law enforcement to collaborate with federal law enforcement to keep our community safe. This ruling guides how we can do that while complying with Colorado law.”

text:
TALLAHASSEE, Florida — Gov. Ron DeSantis’ administration filed evidence Monday that the immigration detention center in the Florida Everglades known as “Alligator Alcatraz” is closed, after a federal judge required proof that the facility had really shut down.

The state offered two declarations, from state employees “intimately familiar” with the status of the facility, who said Alligator Alcatraz no longer exists. One of those testimonies included photographs of the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport, which showed a nearly empty airstrip absent of the hastily constructed detention center that was used to hold thousands of people.

“As is readily apparent from the images, the Facility no longer exists, and there are no detainees on site,” wrote Edward Vincent, a supervisor with the Florida Department of Law Enforcement.

Advertisement

DeSantis’ administration filed the documents as part of an ongoing lawsuit, which was first brought last year over allegations that the government violated detainees’ rights and did not provide them proper access to legal counsel. Now that there are no detainees left at the site, the state has asked the court to find the lawsuit moot.

text:
When the US Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to restrict birthright citizenship, his attention soon turned from the justices to China, prompting a sarcastic social media post.

“I would like to congratulate President Xi, and the Great Country of China, on their massive Birthright Citizenship WIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP,” Trump wrote on social media.

In the hours that followed, the Department of Justice instructed federal prosecutors to prioritise investigations of so-called “birth tourism” schemes. Days later, US House Speaker Mike Johnson said lawmakers were examining legislation addressing women who enter the country to give birth.

The moves suggest that, after losing its constitutional challenge, the Trump administration and its congressional allies are shifting towards immigration enforcement and possible legislation, with China increasingly central to their rhetoric.

Yet no federal data set directly measures how many women enter the United States primarily to give birth, and available figures indicate that births to women living in China represent a minute share of US births.

Trump signed an executive order on his first day back in office, directing federal agencies to deny citizenship documents to children born in the US when their parents were undocumented or present under temporary visas.

name: Human Rights
title: Prost v. Trump - Charity & Security Network
description:
The Parties & Complaint The plaintiffs are independent international ICC judges who authorized or presided over investigations in Palestine and Afghanistan.
The ICC judges are seeking declaratory and injunctive relief to invalidate the enforcement of EO 14203 against them.
This is especially true for those who seek to communicate with ICC personnel by providing human rights expertise and evidence of war crimes.
There have already been legal challenges to EO 14203, such as Smith v. Trump, brought by the ACLU and ACLU of Maine in the United States District Court for the District of Maine on behalf of Matthew Smith and Akila Radhakrishnan.
This case echoes aspects of the litigation brought against the 2020 ICC sanctions, which similarly raised constitutional concerns.
text:
Case Summary

On Jun. 24, 2026, three judges currently sitting on the International Criminal Court (ICC)—Kimberly Prost (Canada), Solomy Bossa (Uganda), and Reine Alapini-Gansour (Benin)—filed a federal lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. They have sued the Trump Administration and are challenging the legality of Executive Order 14203, which declared a “national emergency” and directed the imposition of sanctions and asset freezes against ICC personnel investigating actions by U.S. and Israeli forces and personnel in Gaza.

Executive Order 14203 references the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to target individuals engaged in ICC efforts. Under IEEPA, the President has the authority to impose sanctions on persons or entities upon the determination that there is an “unusual and extraordinary threat, which has its source in whole or substantial part outside the United States, to the national security, foreign policy, or economy of the United States” (50 U.S. Code § 1701). EO 14203, which also cites the authority of the National Emergencies Act (NEA) (50 U.S.C. 1601), the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. 1182(f)), and Section 301 of Title 3, U.S. Code, stating that “any effort by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute” U.S. nationals or U.S. allies constitutes such a threat.

Under EO 14203, any foreign person (including ICC staff and third parties) risks asset blocking and U.S. entry restrictions if they “materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of” an ICC investigation into protected persons. “Protected person” covers U.S. nationals or nationals of U.S. allies (e.g., NATO members, major non-NATO allies) that have refused ICC jurisdiction, and includes U.S. government and its allies’ employees, appointed or elected officials, as well as Armed Forces members and their children and spouses.

EO 14203 does not introduce the concept of covering allied personnel for the first time—a June 2020 EO by the Trump Administration similarly targeted any ICC effort against “personnel of a country that is an ally of the United States.” This earlier EO led to legal challenges, including the Sadat v. Trump case brought by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) on behalf of academics and nonprofits who argued that the EO chilled their constitutionally protected speech and association. In 2021, the Biden Administration ultimately revoked the 2020 sanctions, acknowledging that the measures were “not an effective or appropriate strategy for addressing the United States’ concerns with the ICC.”

The U.S. government claims that since the U.S. and Israel are not parties to the Rome Statute, the ICC has no jurisdiction over personnel of the U.S. or its allies, which is in part the basis of the U.S. sanctions against ICC personnel.

The Parties & Complaint

The plaintiffs are independent international ICC judges who authorized or presided over investigations in Palestine and Afghanistan. Noting that The Open Society Foundations Justice Initiative represents Judge Kimberly Prost in this action; Foley Hoag LLP serves as co-counsel.

The Defendants are the current U.S. Administration, named in the complaint as President Trump, Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent, Todd Blanche, the Department of Justice, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), Bradley Smith, and the State Department.

The ICC judges are seeking declaratory and injunctive relief to invalidate the enforcement of EO 14203 against them. The U.S. government is currently preparing its motion to dismiss and will likely invoke the political question doctrine, lack of standing of the foreign officials, and potentially sovereign immunity.

Main Arguments in the Complaint

The ICC judges presented both constitutional and administrative challenges to the executive branch’s use of emergency powers:

Ultra Vires Actions Exceeding IEEPA Authority

The ICC judges argue that the President exceeded the statutory authority granted by Congress under IEEPA (50 U.S.C. section 1701), which also cites the authority of the National Emergencies Act (NEA) (50 U.S.C. 1601). As noted above, IEEPA requires the presence of an “unusual and extraordinary threat” to the national security, foreign policy, or economy of the United States. The ICC judges argue that a lawful international court carrying out its judicial duties cannot objectively be categorized as a national security threat, and therefore the invocation of IEEPA is a pretextual abuse of power.

The judges also note that IEEPA and the NEA were “designed to limit presidential abuses of emergency authorities, not authorize their unbounded use.” (Complaint, P. 36). They cite Senate Reports and Congressional testimony which demonstrate that the purpose of IEEPA and the NEA was to limit non-wartime powers of the U.S. President. For example, the Complaint cites the “Final Report of the Special Committee on National Emergencies and Delegated Emergency Powers,” which states that the NEA was enacted in 1976 to confront “[r]evelations of how [emergency] power has been abused by high government officials” and “concern about the potential exercise, unchecked by the Congress or the American people, of this extraordinary power.” (Complaint p. 37). The report explicitly writes that the NEA was “not intended to enlarge or add to Executive power.”

Therefore, the judges argue that EO 14203 not only exceeds the bounds of authority set out in IEEPA and the NEA, but they represent exactly the use of broad power that these laws were designed to restrain.

Violations of Fifth Amendment: Due Process & the Takings Clause

The ICC judges assert that they possess protected liberty and property interests under the U.S. Constitution that are affected by the global dominance of the U.S. dollar and financial infrastructure. The sudden freezing of their assets, the closing of their bank accounts, and the cancellation of their health insurance occurred without any notice, a statement of reasons, or a meaningful opportunity to challenge the sanctions, thereby violating due process. The judges call this a “financial death penalty” in the lawsuit, noting they no longer have access to credit cards, banking services, common online platforms like Google and Amazon, health insurance, and are unable to book travel.

The complaint also argues that the blockings of Judges Prost and Bossa’s bank accounts in New York constitute the taking of private property without just compensation under the Fifth Amendment.

Violations of Administrative Procedure Act (APA)

The ICC judges argue that OFAC designation mechanism under the EO is “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law” under 5 U.S.C. Section 706(2)(A) and therefore violates the APA. They contend that the administrative record lacks a rational nexus linking independent judicial work to an immediate national security crisis. The decision on the merits of this argument would also have serious implications for sanctions mechanisms and OFAC transparency in the future.

Infringement on Judicial Independence under Customary Law

The complaint highlights that the sanctions explicitly seek to manipulate or affect ongoing independent judicial officers through intimidation, which conflicts with fundamental international norms that enshrine the independence of the judiciary, which the U.S. has historically recognized and codified.

Implications for Civil Society

Though aimed principally at ICC officials, EO 14203 implicates nonprofits because it creates liability for those who “support or transact” with listed individuals supporting an ICC investigation into “U.S. nationals or nationals of U.S. allies.” This creates a broad chilling effect for nonprofits, lawyers, academics, and other civil society actors. This is especially true for those who seek to communicate with ICC personnel by providing human rights expertise and evidence of war crimes. The potential consequences are significant: willful violations can carry up to 20 years in prison and/or fines up to $1 million.

Fear of these hefty penalties can deter U.S.-based nonprofits from assisting or even communicating with sanctioned ICC staff, effectively stifling documentation of human rights abuses, fact-finding missions, or legal collaboration. It can also make the filing of amicus curiae briefs more perilous, since any direct interaction with ICC proceedings or officials might be construed as “support,” discouraging many nonprofits from contributing valuable legal analysis.

There have already been legal challenges to EO 14203, such as Smith v. Trump, brought by the ACLU and ACLU of Maine in the United States District Court for the District of Maine on behalf of Matthew Smith and Akila Radhakrishnan. In this case, the plaintiffs have argued that EO 14203 unconstitutionally restricts their First Amendment rights by prohibiting their ability to share information and expertise with the ICC’s Office of the Prosecutor. This case echoes aspects of the litigation brought against the 2020 ICC sanctions, which similarly raised constitutional concerns.

Family members of the UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian territories, Francesca Albanese, also brought suit against the Trump Administration for violating their constitutional rights after sanctions were imposed on Albanese under EO 14203 following her communications with the ICC, in which she called for the investigation of war crimes potentially committed by U.S. and Israeli individuals in Gaza.

Until any legal clarifications emerge, the legal exposure and risk of severe penalties will continue deterring civil society from collaborating with the ICC, restricting the flow of critical evidence and expertise that could otherwise contribute to justice for victims of atrocity crimes.

The U.S. government is expected to file a motion to dismiss in response to this complaint. C&SN will continue to monitor the case and update this page.

text:
Carver County has settled with a man who a lawsuit claimed was unlawfully detained by local law enforcement for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after his bail was paid. That's according to court documents, including a settlement filed June 26.

As of Monday, details of the settlement have not been made public.

The American Civil Liberties Union of Minnesota and John Sear, an attorney with the law firm Nelson Mullins, filed the lawsuit in March 2025 on behalf of Maikol Javier Suarez Varela.

According to the complaint, Suarez Varela was arrested in Chanhassen, Minnesota, in January 2025 and taken to the Carver County jail. The complaint said Sheriff Jason Kamerud "or others" working at the jail alerted ICE to his presence at the facility.

ICE then sent the sheriff's office a detainer request, asking it to hold Suarez Varela "up to 48 hours after he would otherwise be released," court documents said.

The ACLU said the Minnesota Freedom Fund posted Suarez Varela's $10,000 bail, but the jail didn't let him go. The lawsuit argued that holding an individual under an ICE detainer is a violation of the Fourth Amendment.

Ian Bratlie, an attorney with the ACLU, said Suarez Varela entered the U.S. lawfully.

At the time the lawsuit was filed, an ICE spokesperson said Suarez Varela was "paroled into the United States" through a port of entry in Texas.

Suarez Varela is not in ICE custody, according to the federal agency's online detainee database.

title: ICE Seeks New Or Bigger Detention Facilities at 14 Sites, Documents Show - TIME
description: As the Trump Administration pushes more arrests, ICE is eyeing detention expansion at 14 sites, documents show, including Guantanamo Bay.
text:
A request for construction proposals published on Friday shows Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is set to expand a detention facility near the U.S.-Mexico border in Port Isabel, Texas. It also lists more than a dozen other potential targets for new or expanded facilities. The tentative list includes plans to revive a detention facility in El Centro, Calif., which was closed in 2014, and to build a facility in St. Thomas in the U.S. Virgin Islands, which does not have any ICE detention facilities.

It also includes a new facility in Guantanamo Bay, the military base in Cuba where Trump announced plans to open an ICE detention facility in January 2025. Trump, at the time, claimed that Guantanamo had “30,000 beds” and promised it would be used to hold “the worst criminal illegal aliens.” But the Administration has so far struggled to deliver on such plans. In May, CBS News reported that the Administration was spending $73 million to operate the immigration detention facility annually, despite it holding only about 400 beds, and fewer than 2% of which were occupied.

Other locations listed for potential facility expansion include Miami; Honolulu; Florence, Arizona; Batavia, New York; Broadview, Illinois; Oakdale, Louisiana; El Paso, Texas; Huntsville, Texas; and Aguadilla, Puerto Rico. It is unclear how ICE will decide which the facilities will ultimately be expanded. One of the documents says the construction plan will move forward "if it is in the government's best interest."

The contract is expected to be awarded by the end of September this year, the document says. TIME has reached out to ICE for comment.

The plan to rapidly expand detention facilities follows a renewed push by the Trump administration to increase immigrant detentions by ICE. A source familiar with the matter tells TIME that the Trump administration recently set a new goal of making 2,000 daily arrests, after failing to meet a goal of 3,000 daily arrests set last year.

But ICE’s initial building spree hit multiple legal and political hurdles, despite Congress appropriating the agency more than $100 billion billions to ramp up its arrests and deportations. ICE previously spent $1 billion purchasing nearly a dozen commercial warehouses in an attempt to convert them into detention facilities. Most of those projects have been stalled by lawsuits challenging the plan's environmental impact on local communities.

The facility routinely violates the Flores Settlement Agreement by detaining children for months past the 20-day limit and using threats of family separation to force migrants to abandon their asylum claims.

The lawmakers highlighted DHS’s violations of court-ordered protections of children’s rights, writing, “The FSA requires that children in immigration custody must be held in the least restrictive setting appropriate to their needs and be detained no longer than 20 days in unlicensed facilities. The Trump Administration consistently and systematically violates these requirements.”

The lawmakers continued by calling on DHS to terminate its contract with CoreCivic and shut down the facility.

text:
The Mexican man who officials say was killed by a truck last week in St. Augustine while running from immigration officers was identified by a farmworkers’ advocacy group as a father of two on vacation with a valid tourist visa.

Juan Jairo Coronilla Duran, 28, was visiting from his hometown of San Luis de La Paz, a small city in the central state of Guanajuato, according to Orlando-based non-profit Colectivo Árbol. Officials have yet to confirm his identity.

Isaret Jeffers, who represents the organization and has been providing support to his wife, Jessica Alamilla, said Coronilla Duran arrived in the United States three weeks ago for vacation, and had only been in Florida for two days. He was hit and killed by the truck on July 14.

“He was going to return this past Saturday. He had already bought a flight,” Jeffers said. “Now, unfortunately, if he is returning, his return is different.”

READ MORE: Mexican man is killed by truck as he flees immigration agents in St. Augustine

The Florida Highway Patrol told the Miami Herald last week that the agency found he had been running from an encounter with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Homeland Security Investigations agents. DHS has not provided new details since the incident took place last week.

His was the third death following an encounter with immigration officials in a week, after federal agents shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican man in Houston on July 7, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian man, in Biddeford, Maine on July 13. Neither of the men were the targets of the agents.

As the Trump Administration carries out a sweeping mass deportation campaign, agents are rounding up immigrants on sidewalks, highways and in homes, some with work permits and other legal documentation. U.S. citizens have also been stopped and detained.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has opened an investigation into the deaths of at least 18 Mexican nationals since Trump assumed office, some of whom died during arrests and others in immigration detention. She said her government wants to file criminal charges.

“We express our deepest solidarity and sincere condolences to the family of the victims. Their pain is shared by the entire nation,” Sheinbaum said on July 14. “No fellow citizen should be unprotected when facing possible abuse from authority, disproportionate use of force, or human rights violations.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security declined to provide further details of last week’s incident in St. Augustine.

“On July 14, DHS law enforcement conducted an operation near St. Johns, Florida. Florida Highway Patrol and HSI are investigating an incident resulting in the death of a Mexican national,” read a statement sent again to the Herald on Monday. “We will provide an update when available.”

Coronilla Duran’s wife found out about his death while watching television, Jeffers said. Alamilla declined a request to be interviewed, and Jeffers said she is focused on returning home with his body.

Alamilla hadn’t heard from her husband in more than a day when she saw the news that a man had been killed, and feared it was him. The couple have been married for 10 years and have a seven-month-old daughter and a seven-year-old son, Jeffers said. They own a small business in San Luis de La Paz.

Alamilla flew to Florida on Friday to make arrangements with a local funeral home, Jeffers said, while relatives watched their children. On Monday, she worked with the Mexican consulate to take his body back home to Mexico.

Of the Mexicans who have died in ICE custody or during arrests, at least four died by presumed suicide, including 19-year-old Royer Perez-Jimenez in March in Florida.

Jeffers said that Colectivo Árbol mainly supports farmworkers, many of whom are afraid to leave their homes amid immigration arrests.

“People are too afraid to go out and do things that used to be normal, like going to the supermarket, taking their kids to the park,” Jeffers said. “None of that is happening anymore.”

Unmarked blue SUVs

Jose Rivera, a truck driver for a garbage collection company, witnessed Coronilla Duran run out of the gas station in front of a Wawa convenience store off the highway.

Rivera had stopped for breakfast, and was sitting in his truck parallel to the highway just before 7 a.m. Coronilla Duran wore a light sky blue hoodie over a white T-shirt, blue jeans and Timberland shoes, he said.

Coronilla Duran ran to the sidewalk leading to State Road 16 and turned around. Rivera followed Coronilla Duran’s gaze in his truck’s rearview mirror to see what he was running from.

“That’s when I see the undercover car with the lights on,” Rivera said. “But when I looked back, he started running across the road.”

Rivera said he saw unmarked blue SUVs with tinted windows stopped on either side of a car at the gas station, and one moved to follow Coronilla Duran. The agents were in green uniforms, he said, and he thought they were from St. Johns County Sheriff’s Office. But the sheriff’s office told the Herald it wasn’t involved in the incident, and responded later to investigate the traffic accident.

Rivera said Coronilla Duran reached the median of the highway, a small strip of grass, slipped and fell, picked himself up, and stumbled onto the asphalt of the other lane of traffic.

“The traffic was coming pretty quick, and he just lost his footing and didn’t look where the traffic was coming,” Rivera said. “He kept looking back.”

Rivera watched as the man fell in front of a trailer-tractor, and knew instantly that he had died.

Agents didn’t notice at first, Rivera thought, because he saw an officer point to the woods on the other side, as if they thought he escaped. But then they noticed the body in the road.

“It was a heartbreaking moment for me,” Rivera said. “I have kids around his age.”

Officers began to close off the road, and Rivera drove off. When he later heard the man’s age he found it hard to believe. He looked younger, in the brief second Rivera glimpsed his face.

“I hate when things like that happen, especially to young ones,” Rivera told the Herald. “I’m almost 60, and yeah, you know, I’ve been through a lot of life, but everybody should make it until they’re older, right?”

title: Senators demand ICE answers and body cameras after deadly shootings in Maine and Houston
description:
The demands follow two deadly shootings in which ICE officers shot and killed immigrants in Houston and Maine.
Hundreds of pages of family court documents describe their turbulent marriage, and the years after.
READ MORE: Lawmakers demand answers after 'bombshell' report of ICE officer shooting in Maine In court filings, David Brouillette said that his second ex-wife had slandered him.
The shootings in Maine and Houston both involved ICE officers shooting at people who were in vehicles at the time.
In the wake of the Maine shooting, Homeland Security temporarily stopped officers from conducting vehicle stops except in specific situations.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Dozens of Democratic U.S. senators and the Independent senator from Maine pushed for more details Monday from Immigration and Customs Enforcement about the agency's vetting practices for new agents and how officers conduct vehicle pursuits, even as they demanded that body cameras be swiftly rolled out to all officers.

The demands came in a letter spearheaded by Maine's Independent Sen. Angus King, signed by 38 Democratic senators and sent to the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE. The demands follow two deadly shootings in which ICE officers shot and killed immigrants in Houston and Maine.

The Associated Press reported last week that the ICE officer in Maine who opened fire and killed a man from Colombia had a history of violent behavior toward family members that was detailed in family court records.

His first ex-wife, Ashley Brouillette, told AP he was physically violent with her, including once throwing boiling water at her while she was holding their child.

His second ex-wife, Lucinda Brouillette, sent a statement over the weekend alleging "a persistent pattern of abuse, intimidation, manipulation, fear, and control."

"Throughout our marriage and in the years that followed, I have feared for a long time that his anger, aggression, and escalating behavior would eventually result in severe, life threatening violence, and I often believed I would be the one on the receiving end of it," she wrote.

Hundreds of pages of family court documents describe their turbulent marriage, and the years after. Lucinda Brouillette told the court he had stalked and harassed her and physically and verbally abused his daughter, according to multiple requests for temporary protection orders. Brouillette tackled his teenage daughter and smashed spaghetti in her hair, and during another outburst, he dragged his daughter around the house as she cried, she said.

"Dave needs counseling or something for his PTSD & depression," she wrote in an application for a temporary protective order on behalf of his teenage daughter which a judge granted in 2021.

READ MORE: Lawmakers demand answers after 'bombshell' report of ICE officer shooting in Maine

In court filings, David Brouillette said that his second ex-wife had slandered him.

Multiple family members told the AP the government should have never given him a gun, badge and the authority to patrol city streets as the Trump administration ramps up its mass deportation agenda.

The senators' letter on Monday listed new measures to increase accountability at the agency, including transparency about whether ICE considers records from family court of domestic violence or abuse when vetting new recruits.

"We remain supportive of removing dangerous convicted criminals from our communities, but this goal can and must be achieved without endangering these very communities in the process. By no stretch could either of the victims in Texas and Maine be characterized as 'the worst of the worst,' making these tragic deaths even more egregious," the senators wrote. "The American people deserve clarity and accountability."

They said ICE should immediately start wearing uniforms or vests that clearly identify them as "ICE" instead of the more generic "POLICE" or "POLICE ICE." Civil rights groups and advocates have often criticized ICE for not wearing uniforms or clear identification on their ballistics vests identifying them as deportation officers.

Senators also demanded to know what changes were being made to how officers conduct traffic stops and vehicle pursuits.

The shootings in Maine and Houston both involved ICE officers shooting at people who were in vehicles at the time. In the wake of the Maine shooting, Homeland Security temporarily stopped officers from conducting vehicle stops except in specific situations. But just a day later, after fierce criticism from some MAGA supporters, President Donald Trump said on social media that traffic stops should continue.

Homeland Security said last week that it was adding new training in crowd-control measures, high-risk vehicle stops, live-fire exercises and medical training, in response to what they called coordinated attacks against their officers and ICE facilities.

text:
COLUMBUS – Late Friday, a federal judge in the Southern District of Ohio dismissed a class action lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Customs and Border Protection(CBP), and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which sought an injunction to prohibit federal agencies from conducting warrantless arrests without probable cause. Although Judge Morrison found that Defendants have “authorized a widespread and persistent pattern of illegal warrantless arrests in Ohio”, the dismissal states that Plaintiffs did not establish that they presented an imminent risk of future unlawful arrests in Ohio.

The ACLU of Ohio, CRIS, ABLE, along with local co-counsel, filed the class action complaint on March 18, and presented evidence to Chief Judge Sarah Morrison during a three-day preliminary injunction hearing in early June.

“This ruling is deeply disappointing and frustrating but also recognizes that federal agents are wantonly conducting haphazard arrests in violation of the clear dictates of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA). Federal immigration agents are required, by federal law, to either effectuate a warranted arrest, or, without a warrant, find probable cause of removability and likelihood of escape before an arrest. Last week’s decision reaffirms these clear dictates and proves that federal agents are not above the law. The ACLU of Ohio remains steadfast in our commitment to protecting immigrants’ rights and we will continue to pursue justice on behalf of immigrant members of our community,” -Freda Levenson, ACLU of Ohio Chief Legal Officer.

“The opinion from the Court confirms what we already knew: ICE violated the law and arrested our clients illegally. Unfortunately, we are living in a world where documented human rights violations alone are insufficient to compel court action to stop them. ICE's presence here continues to grow, and as advocates on the front lines, we continue to witness these same violations happening in real time. Court intervention would have been welcome, but its absence changes nothing about our resolve to continue finding ways to defend our immigrant neighbors, ” -Angela K. Plummer, Executive Director, Community Refugee & Immigration Services (CRIS).

title: DHS and Department of Justice Announce Move to Revoke U.S. Citizenship from 10 ...
description:

text:
The Trump Administration continues the largest denaturalization effort ever

WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS), alongside the Department of Justice (DOJ), announced denaturalization actions in various U.S. district courts against 10 individuals accused of serious offenses—including sexual abuse of a child, health care and wire fraud, immigration fraud, and conspiracy to possess with the intent to distribute cocaine. The complaints were filed over the last 30 days.

Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, a naturalized U.S. citizen’s citizenship may be revoked, and certificate of naturalization canceled, if the naturalization was illegally procured or procured by concealment of a material fact or by willful misrepresentation.

“When you commit fraud during the naturalization process, you forfeit the right to keep your U.S. citizenship,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “These criminal aliens, comprised of drug traffickers, pedophiles, and fraudsters, lost that right and exploited our immigration system—harming real U.S. citizens. DHS is committed to ensuring we denaturalize and remove these fraudsters with every tool at our disposal.”

“These ten criminal aliens — including child sex abusers, a nearly $900,000 Medicare fraudster, and a cocaine trafficker — lied their way into U.S. citizenship,” said Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Each of these individuals lacked the good moral character required by law and procured citizenship through willful misrepresentations and concealment of their crimes. Under President Trump’s leadership, this Department of Justice will continue to aggressively pursue denaturalization to restore integrity to America’s naturalization process.”

“We refuse to give a free pass to criminals who cheated their way into American citizenship,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “Under this administration, if you defrauded the naturalization process, you will face the full force of the Justice Department. We’ve only scratched the surface — many more complaints are coming.”

1. Yoskmaikel Rodriguez Perez (Age 45/Cuba): Rodriguez Perez, a native of Cuba, became a lawful permanent resident in 2004 and naturalized as a U.S. citizen in 2018. Before obtaining citizenship, however, Rodriguez Perez operated a purported medical clinic and submitted false and fraudulent claims to Medicare in excess of $886,694. Rodriguez Perez concealed this criminal conduct throughout the naturalization process and provided false testimony under oath to a U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) officer. Rodriguez Perez later pleaded guilty and was convicted of conspiracy to commit healthcare and wire fraud. On June 18, 2026, the United States filed a four-count denaturalization action in the Southern District of Florida. The complaint alleges that Rodriguez Perez illegally procured his citizenship because he lacked the good moral character required for naturalization given his crime of moral turpitude, unlawful acts, and false testimony under oath during the naturalization process; and because he procured U.S. citizenship through the concealment of material facts and willful misrepresentations.

2. Ceflo Luviano-Mojica (Age 60/Mexico): On July 14, 2026, the United States brought a denaturalization action against Ceflo Luviano-Mojica, a native of Mexico, who misrepresented his prior arrest for Carrying a Concealed Firearm and for Grand Theft, for which he spent 30 days in jail. In 1998, Luviano pleaded guilty and was convicted in the Northern District of Georgia of, inter alia, Providing False Information in a Naturalization Application, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 1015. Luviano admitted he had made a false statement both on his naturalization application and during his interview, when he testified under oath that he had never been arrested, charged, or imprisoned for breaking or violating any law. The United States filed a two-count denaturalization action in the Northern District of Georgia alleging that Luviano illegally procured his citizenship by lacking the good moral character required for naturalization and procuring U.S. citizenship through the concealment of material facts and willful misrepresentations.

3. Urbano Vazquez Ortega (Age 53/Mexico): On July 10, 2026, the United States brought a denaturalization action against Urbano Vazquez Ortega, who sexually assaulted children while employed as a priest in a Washington, D.C. church. Mr. Vazquez Ortega is a native of Mexico and was naturalized as a U.S. citizen on July 11, 2017. Mr. Vazquez Ortega was charged with, and convicted in the Superior Court for the District of Columbia of multiple counts of Second-Degree Child Sexual Abuse. Between 2015 to 2017, Mr. Vazquez Ortega touched the breasts, genitalia, and buttocks of his victims and in one instance thrusted his tongue into the mouth of a minor female victim. In 2019, Mr. Vazquez Ortega was sentenced to fifteen years in prison and is presently incarcerated. The United States filed a five-count complaint against Mr. Vazquez Ortega to revoke his naturalized citizenship as he committed these crimes before, during, and after his naturalization as a U.S. citizen.

4. Murtaza Ali (Age 65/Pakistan): Ali is a native of Pakistan who filed multiple applications for immigration benefits under different aliases until he obtained a grant of an immigration benefit under the alias “Muhammad Iqbal.” Ali, through the grant of the immigration benefit, obtained permanent residency under the alias “Muhammad Iqbal” and thereafter naturalized under this alias in 2009. Following Ali’s naturalization, a fingerprint expert determined that the fingerprints provided with immigration benefits applications filed under the names “Mortaza Ali” and “Muhammad Iqbal” were made by the same person. As a result, the United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas charged Ali with making False Material Statements to an Agency of the United States in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 1001. In 2014, Ali pleaded guilty as charged, admitting that he had filed three separate applications for immigration benefits using three different identities. On July 14, 2026, the United States filed a four-count denaturalization action in the Northern District of Texas alleging that Ali procured his citizenship by committing immigration fraud, engaging in unlawful acts that reflect adversely on his moral character, providing false testimony under oath during the naturalization process, and procuring citizenship through the concealment of material facts and willful misrepresentations.

5. Jimmy Aguero (Age 51/Peru): Mr. Aguero repeatedly sexually abused his minor stepdaughter prior to naturalizing as a U.S. citizen on October 6, 2015. A jury found Aguero guilty on EIGHT counts of the sexual abuse of a minor, and he was sentenced to ten years of imprisonment. The Department of Justice filed a complaint alleging that Mr. Aguero was statutorily barred from showing that he was a person of good moral character because of his convictions. The Department also alleged that he procured his naturalization by concealment of material facts.

6. Antonio Alcantara-Ruiz (Age 53/Mexico): On June 23, 2026, the United States brought a denaturalization action against Antonio Alcantara-Ruiz, a/k/a Emiliano Quintana-Gonzalez, a/k/a Antonio Quinn Alcantara, who misrepresented his identity to secure citizenship. Prior to the naturalization process, Alcantara purchased identity documents from a fellow Mexican citizen and used those documents to secure a replacement permanent resident card which contained Alcantara-Ruiz’s picture and fingerprint. Alcantara-Ruiz then used the false documents in support of his naturalization. The United States filed a 4-count complaint against Alcantara-Ruiz seeking to cancel his naturalized citizenship.

7. Omar Cantu-Montalvo (Age 44/Mexico): Cantu-Montalvo was admitted to the United States in March 1996 and subsequently obtained permanent residence. When he applied to naturalize in July 2005, Mr. Cantu-Montalvo stated in his application that he had never committed a crime or offense for which he had not been arrested. He later repeated that claim during his naturalization interview. His application was approved, and he naturalized in December 2005. In April 2016, however, Mr. Cantu-Montalvo pleaded guilty in federal district court to conspiracy to possess with the intent to distribute more than 5 kilograms of cocaine—a conspiracy he joined in April 2005, just a few months before he applied for naturalization. For his crime, the court sentenced Mr. Cantu-Montalvo to 100 months of imprisonment followed by a five-year term of supervised release. On June 15, 2026, the United States filed a complaint seeking to revoke Mr. Cantu-Montalvo’s citizenship because he illegally procured his citizenship as he was unable to demonstrate good moral character in light of his commission of a controlled substance offense. Additionally, Mr. Cantu-Montalvo is subject to denaturalization because he willfully misrepresented or concealed his offense while seeking United States citizenship.

8. Franscisco Montano (Age 59/Mexico): Montano was legally admitted to the United States in February of 1987, but when he applied to naturalize in 1997, Montano failed to divulge that he had sexual abused a child during the mandatory five-year good moral character period prior to the naturalization process. Montano was later convicted in a Texas State court of two counts of Aggravated Sexual assault and four counts of Indecency with a Child that occurred during the five-year period. As Montano should not have been naturalized, the United States filed a complaint on June 30 in the Southern District of Texas to revoke his illegally-obtained citizenship.

9. Marcin Stanislaw Garbacz (Age 47/Poland): Garbacz, a native of Poland and former Roman Catholic priest, became a lawful permanent resident in 2008 and naturalized as a U.S. citizen in 2014. Before obtaining citizenship, Garbacz engaged in a scheme to steal approximately $259,696 in cash collections from three parishes within the Diocese of Rapid City, South Dakota. Garbacz also secretly recorded a 17-year-old showering during a church trip to Poland. Garbacz concealed this criminal conduct throughout the naturalization process. Garbacz was later convicted of multiple federal offenses, including wire fraud, making and subscribing a false tax return, and engaging in illicit sexual conduct in a foreign place involving a minor. text:
On July 15, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island denied the federal government’s request to stay the court’s earlier ruling in Dorcas International Institute of Rhode Island v. USCIS, pending its appeal. This means that USCIS must continue to process and adjudicate immigration applications and petitions from the 39 affected countries while the government’s appeal moves forward.

Prior Ruling and USCIS Statement

On June 5, 2026, the court held that USCIS exceeded its statutory authority by implementing policies that effectively halted the adjudication of immigration benefits for nationals of designated “travel ban” countries. The court found that these policies violated both the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

Specifically, the court vacated policies that suspended adjudication of many applications and petitions filed on behalf of nationals of designated countries, paused certain asylum-related adjudications, required re-review of previously approved immigration benefits and directed adjudicators to treat an applicant’s country of origin as a significant negative discretionary factor.

On June 12, 2026, after the court directed that USCIS detail the concrete steps it had taken to comply with the court order, USCIS announced that the policy memoranda placing an adjudicatory hold on cases from the affected countries would be treated as if they are no longer in effect, pending further litigation.

Latest Update: Stay Denied

On June 12, the Department of Justice filed an appeal and requested a stay to halt the court’s June 5 order during the appellate process. By denying this stay on July 15, 2026, the court ensures that the original ruling lifting the hold on adjudications, remains fully active and that USCIS is legally required to continue adjudication of affected cases while the higher court reviews the case.

The processing mandate applies to:

Adjustment of status applications

Nonimmigrant and Immigrant Visa Petitions

Employment authorization requests

Naturalization applications

Certain asylum-related benefits.

Impact on Employers and Next Steps

Employers should review pending petitions or applications for employees from affected countries. As USCIS works through backlogged files, employers should expect to receive final adjudications and should also be prepared to receive potential Requests for Evidence (RFEs), interview notices and/or biometric appointments.
