text:
From the outset of President Trump’s second term, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has engaged in a deadly immigration crackdown that has trampled the constitutional rights of migrants and US citizens.

During the operation, there have been 28 incidents where immigration agents shot at people, resulting in eight deaths, according to an analysis by The Trace. On July 13, an ICE officer fatally shot Joan Sebastian Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old delivery driver from Colombia authorized to work in the US. On July 7, an ICE officer shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a father of three who worked in the US for more than three decades.

According to federal courts, ICE agents have repeatedly violated the rights of citizens, stopping people for “looking Mexican,” conducting warrantless raids, and ignoring due process. Peaceful protestors and journalists have been targeted with chemical agents, rubber bullets, and flash grenades. Since January 2025, at least 52 people have died in ICE custody from a variety of causes, including medical neglect and homicide.

While this dragnet reflects the priorities of Trump and his top advisors, it cannot persist in a vacuum. It requires broader political and economic support. The political support for ICE has come from Congress, which has both massively increased ICE’s funding and repeatedly failed to rein in its excesses.

Popular Information identified the core of ICE’s Congressional support by cataloging members of Congress who, looking at this record, have sought to increase ICE’s power by sponsoring or co-sponsoring pending legislation. This includes bills like the “10 Years of ICE Funding Act,” sponsored by Senator Eric Schmitt (R-MO), and co-sponsored by Josh Hawley (R-MO) and Bernie Moreno (R-OH), which provides $105 billion in dedicated funding for ICE through 2036. And the “287(g) Cooperation Act of 2026,” sponsored by Congressman Ben Cline (R-VA) and co-sponsored by 16 Republican colleagues, which conditions federal public safety funding for state and local governments on the signing of a cooperation agreement with ICE within 180 days.

Overall, 40 bills — including 27 House bills and 13 Senate bills — were included in the analysis. (A complete list of those bills, and their sponsors, is available here.)

In total, Popular Information has identified 110 House members and 37 Senators who have sponsored or co-sponsored at least one of the 40 bills expanding ICE’s power during the 119th Congress. The most prolific supporter of these bills was Congressman Barry Moore (R-AL), who sponsored or co-sponsored 12. Following close behind were Congresswoman Nancy Mace (R-SC) and Congressman Brandon Gill (R-TX), who each sponsored or co-sponsored nine. In the Senate, Eric Schmitt (R-MO) sponsored or co-sponsored seven such bills, with Rick Scott (R-FL) sponsoring or co-sponsoring five.

Popular Information then analyzed corporate PAC donations reported to the FEC during the 2026 political cycle to the campaign committees and leadership PACs of these members.

The top consumer brand financially backing this group of ICE supporters is SpaceX, Elon Musk’s newly public company that runs Starlink satellite internet, xAI’s Grok chatbot, and the X social media platform. SpaceX’s corporate PAC donated $589,000 to 63 members of Congress who sponsored or co-sponsored legislation expanding ICE’s power. Other consumer brands near the top of the list include Home Depot ($536,500 to 77 members), Walmart ($308,000 to 88 members), Toyota ($262,500 to 75 members), and Google ($257,500 to 48 members).

In the first Trump administration, some of the companies on the list opposed Trump’s immigration policies, including those targeting the undocumented. In 2017, for example, the CEOs of Amazon, Google, Microsoft, AT&T, and Walmart all signed a letter calling for legislation to protect undocumented immigrants who were brought to the US as children. During the second administration, none of these companies have publicly opposed any of Trump’s immigration policies.

text:
A proposed $100,000 green card applicant bond for some immigrants seeking permanent residence in the United States could trigger legal challenges over whether the Trump administration has the authority to impose such a financial requirement, experts said.

The proposal, first reported by The Wall Street Journal, would require some immigrant visa applicants applying through U.S. consulates abroad to post a bond that could reach $100,000. The Trump administration has tightened control around legal immigration pathways to make things more difficult and expensive for immigrants.

State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Newsweek in a statement over email that President Donald Trump "has made clear that those who wish to immigrate to the United States must be financially self-sufficient."

Read More on News

Pigott said the State Department is working with the Department of Homeland Security to explore the use of existing immigration authorities that allow officials to require bonds in certain cases involving applicants who may be considered likely to become a public charge.

"This commonsense solution serves a dual purpose—preserving public assistance resources for hardworking Americans while giving applicants who have the resources to pay their own way another option to demonstrate their self-sufficiency and qualify for a U.S. visa," Pigott said.

Immigration attorney Charles Kuck told Newsweek any effort to expand bond requirements to green card applicants would almost certainly face legal challenges, even though federal immigration law contains provisions allowing the government to require bonds in some public-charge cases.

Kuck said the administration would likely rely on existing federal immigration law, including provisions that allow bonds in certain public-charge cases.

"There's daylight between 'bond tied to an individualized public-charge determination' and 'bond imposed categorically based on nationality or country-of-origin risk factors,'" Kuck said.

Kuck said a requirement applied broadly across immigrant visa categories, rather than based on individual assessments, could face challenges in court.

"If the administration tries to import the nationality-based, categorical approach into the immigrant visa context rather than tying bonds to individualized public-charge findings, that's a much weaker fit with the statute and a real point of vulnerability. Either way, there will be lawsuits."

Kuck said opponents of the administration's new bond would likely argue that immigration law does not authorize blanket bond requirements for broad categories of immigrant visa applicants. Other challenges could focus on how the policy is implemented, including whether the administration follows the federal rulemaking process and adequately explains its reasoning.

He said challengers are also likely to argue that the proposal is unnecessary because immigration law already includes safeguards designed to ensure new immigrants can support themselves financially, including existing public-charge screening and financial sponsorship requirements.

Supporters of the proposal argue that bonds could provide an additional way for applicants to demonstrate they have the financial resources to support themselves and reduce potential costs to public benefit programs.

The proposal is still under consideration, and it remains unclear when or whether the administration will implement the requirement or which immigrant visa categories would be affected.

The bond amount could vary depending on individual circumstances and could be set above or below $100,000, according to people familiar with the discussions cited by The Wall Street Journal. Officials are considering initially testing the proposal with applicants from a limited number of countries as a pilot program, the newspaper reported.

Under the proposal, applicants would likely receive the money back only after becoming U.S. citizens, a process that generally takes at least five years, according to The Wall Street Journal. The bond would serve as financial security if an immigrant later required public assistance, the outlet reported. Family members may also be allowed to post the bond on behalf of an applicant, per the report.

The proposed green card bond requirement comes after the administration previously sought to impose a $100,000 payment requirement for certain H-1B visa petitions, a policy that was blocked by a federal judge after it was challenged in court.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration is pursuing a series of changes to how immigration officials evaluate whether applicants are likely to become a "public charge." Earlier this month, the administration moved to revive a policy allowing immigration officers to consider an applicant's use of certain public benefits, including Medicaid, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits, and housing assistance, when deciding some green card applications.

Adam Klein, a former senior Department of Homeland Security (DHS) official, said the green card bond proposal raises questions about how the government would implement a new financial requirement within the existing immigration system.

"The more interesting question is whether Congress intended that authority to be used this way," Klein told Newsweek. He said immigrant visa applicants already go through a detailed process that includes financial sponsorship requirements, inadmissibility reviews and extensive screening, and that adding a bond would create another layer to that system.

Klein said the administration would also need to consider how bond decisions are made, whether standards are applied consistently across U.S. consulates and whether applicants have a meaningful process to challenge those decisions.

"The biggest policy question is a practical one: What problem is the bond intended to solve? Congress has already established financial sponsorship requirements, public charge provisions, and extensive screening for immigrant visas. If the administration believes those tools are no longer sufficient, I think it will need to clearly explain why and how a bond advances the objectives Congress intended," Klein said.

text:
For as long as I’ve taught National Security Law, the Alien Terrorist Removal Court (“ATRC”), a specialized national security court that Congress created in 1996, has been a recurring curiosity of mine. Last week, it was activated for the first time in its 30 years of existence. Congress’ idea in creating the ATRC was to provide a judicial mechanism for removal proceedings that functions like the one provided by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), in which the government could simultaneously (1) obtain meaningful judicial review in a deportation case; while (2) keeping the (classified) evidence secret. Indeed, in a 2014 book chapter, my now-colleague David Cole and I held out the ATRC procedure as a potentially useful illustration of the “cleared counsel” model of national security litigation—in which, instead of providing the subject of an enforcement proceeding with the classified information on which the proceeding depends, the government provides it to a lawyer for the subject (albeit in only a subset of cases before the ATRC). As the chapter reflects, the ATRC had remained an academic curiosity—because it had never actually been used—until last week.

On Friday, Seamus Hughes (the truly indispensable editor of “Court Watch,” among many other things) broke the news that the Trump administration had filed the first-ever application before the ATRC, leading to the first order in that court’s 30-year history (and its hasty creation of a website). We don’t know much beyond what Seamus has already reported (and what’s now on the ATRC’s website). We don’t know the identity of the person subject to the proceedings, why the government believes this person is an “alien terrorist,” what evidence the government is relying on to make that case to the ATRC, or why it chose that route instead of the normal immigration removal process (other than, presumably, to keep the evidence secret). But as someone who has spent more time thinking about the ATRC than, I suspect, 99.99% of the population, now seems as good a time as any to introduce the court; to flag the constitutional questions its statutory structure raises; and to reflect on how alarming it is that the Trump administration has, after all this time, activated it.

Skipping to the punchline, much like the FISA Court, the ATRC reflects a series of imperfect compromises. And there are reasons to worry about some of the benefits that the ATRC process provides to the government. But—and this is the important part—it also has some protections baked into it that are not currently available (or, at least, not immediately available) to many non-citizens in the “regular” removal process, primarily the robust role of Article III district judges—as opposed to Justice Department immigration judges—in administering it.

And there are reasons to worry about some of the benefits that the ATRC process provides to the government. But—and this is the important part—it also has some protections baked into it that are not currently available (or, at least, not immediately available) to many non-citizens in the “regular” removal process, primarily the robust role of Article III district judges—as opposed to Justice Department immigration judges—in administering it.

I have at least some concerns about why the Trump administration is dusting it off now. But there’s no universe in which the ATRC will allow the administration to pursue the kind of mass, summary deportations that it has thus far been unable to achieve through any other immigration authorities. If there’s something nefarious afoot, it’s meaningfully smaller than that in scale.

Unpacking the ATRC

In 1996, as part of the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act (and as quickly amended in the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act), Congress created the ATRC—a tribunal largely modeled on the FISA Court, and which was intended to be able to handle individual deportation hearings in cases involving highly sensitive national security information. Although the statutory procedures are quite complex, the Federal Judicial Center has a helpful summary:

The statute authorize[s] the Attorney General to draft an application for removal of a suspected alien terrorist [a term defined by statute], and to submit the application to the removal court under seal. A single judge may grant the application upon a finding that the alien in question has been identified correctly as an alien terrorist present in the United States and that removal under other available legal means would pose a risk to national security. Upon granting a removal application, the court must hold a public removal hearing at which the accused has the right to be represented by counsel and the government bears the burden of proving that the accused is an alien terrorist. To avoid the disclosure of classified information, the government must prepare an unclassified summary of such information which the judge must find to be sufficient for the alien to prepare a defense. If the government meets its burden of proof at the hearing, the court will order the alien removed from the United States.

As for the judges, the ATRC is composed of five already-serving Article III district judges “assigned” by the Chief Justice to also serve on that court, the only criterion for which is that they come from five different circuits. (For more on the Chief Justice’s assignment powers, see the trivia, below). Under the 1996 statute, the Chief Justice may assign to the ATRC judges who are also serving on the FISA Court, but he doesn’t have to (all five of the current ATRC judges are also FISA judges, but that hasn’t always been true).

The Attorney General can appeal a judge’s denial of an application under the statute, and either the Attorney General or the non-citizen at issue may appeal the decision of the judge after a removal hearing. Unlike the FISA process (where there’s also a specialized appeals court—the FISA Court of Review), the 1996 statute gives the ordinary D.C. Circuit exclusive appellate jurisdiction over the ATRC.

I started with the judges and the appeals process because this is probably the most important point about the ATRC: The compromise it reflects is one in which the government’s benefits involve the protection of classified information and the burden of proof (about which more shortly), but in which the costs sound almost entirely in who is reviewing these cases. (There are also some more pro-government rules respecting detention of the subject of the hearing both beforehand and afterwards, but the daylight between those rules and the rules in “ordinary” cases has shrunk quite a bit since 1996.) Unlike immigration judges housed within the Justice Department’s Executive Office of Immigration Review (who are less and less independent by the day), the ATRC is staffed not just by Article III district judges, but (especially today) by those with experience handling the only comparable kind of litigation—classified applications and other proceedings brought under FISA.

The ATRC’s Chief Judge, Judge Joan Ericksen (a senior judge on the District of Minnesota), made this abundantly clear in the order she publicly issued on Thursday. Here’s the relevant text:

On July 15, 2026, the United States filed an Application to the United States Alien Terrorist Removal Court pursuant to 8 U.S.C. § 1531 et seq. to remove the respondent in the above-captioned matter from the United States. On July 16, 2026, the Court held a hearing as contemplated by § 1533(c)(1), at which the Court heard attorney argument but no sworn testimony was taken. During the hearing the United States offered to supplement the record with information, and the Court had questions about the nexus that the government alleges between the actions of the respondent and the specific sections and subsections it invokes with respect to those actions. The answers persuaded the Court that the Government could benefit from the opportunity for more thoughtful consideration.

In other words, the ATRC is not going to be a rubber stamp.

Constitutional Concerns with the ATRC

That said, it’s also worth highlighting the constitutional concerns militating in the other direction, most of which were flagged (and carefully analyzed) in an excellent 2008 student note in the Duke Law Journal by John Dorsett Niles. The biggest ones involve the evidence. If the cost to the government of the ATRC process is an Article III judge and a D.C. Circuit appeal, the benefit is the ability to rely entirely on evidence that will remain classified—and be presented in most cases only to the judge and only in camera.

If the judge, after considering the evidence on the record as a whole, finds that the government has met its burden (i.e., that a preponderance of the evidence shows the non-citizen to be an “alien terrorist,” as that term is defined, rather broadly by statute), the judge shall order the alien removed and detained pending removal from the United States. If the alien was released pending the removal hearing, the judge shall order the Attorney General to take the alien into custody.

In other words, the statute authorizes the government to remove someone from the country based on evidence the person being removed never sees and doesn’t meaningfully have an opportunity to contest. As Niles’s note points out, this raises quite severe due process questions—especially for those non-citizens whose due process rights most closely approximate those of citizens, i.e., lawful, permanent residents (LPRs, or “Green Card” holders).

Mindful of those concerns, Congress provided a special procedure for cases in which the subject of the proceeding is an LPR. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1534(e)(3)(F), the court in such a case must appoint a “special attorney to assist the alien,” “by reviewing in camera the classified information on behalf of the alien, and . . . by challenging through an in camera proceeding the veracity of the evidence contained in the classified information.” In other words, an LPR is entitled to have a lawyer challenge the evidence being used against them, even if the lawyer can’t actually consult with the subject of the proceeding. This approach is obviously not perfect, but it reflects at least a genuine attempt on Congress’s part to balance the government’s interest against that of the non-citizen.

At the other end of the spectrum from LPRs, for better or worse (my own view skews toward the latter), non-citizens with far weaker claims to comparable due process protections (including those who have never had lawful immigration status) can be removed from the country under this provision without ever being told why; other than the government, only the judge assigned to the case (and the D.C. Circuit if the judge’s decision is challenged) would ever know the reasons. And in the middle, perhaps the hardest cases are those in which the subject is a non-citizen with substantial lawful connections to the United States, just not LPR status. Those individuals would have the strongest argument, in my view, that the statute fails to accord them the constitutionally required process—because they don’t get the benefit of the “special attorney” even though they have substantial due process rights.

As Niles notes, the seriousness of these constitutional concerns is almost certainly a big part of why, across 30 years, the government had never previously utilized this procedure. And we have no way to know what it is that prompted the Trump administration to change course now. But it seems worth flagging three things that we do know—which ought to bear on both how big a story this is and how alarmed we should be by it.

What We Know and What to Watch For

First, on its face, the statute contemplates a robust and meaningful role for the district judge—in lieu of the subject and their attorney in most cases. And Thursday’s order by Chief Judge Ericksen is a promising sign that she, at least, takes that role seriously. Of course, a different judge could handle things differently – there is no track record yet, and it remains to be seen whether this case will be an outlier. Courts could do a lot, in this context, to mitigate the constitutional concerns by ensuring not only that the government is held to the statutory requirements in every particular, but that its evidence that the subject really is an “alien terrorist” is robust and substantial.

Second, because of the meaningful (if secret) judicial review the statute contemplates, there is no universe in which the ATRC could become a vehicle for mass, summary deportations along the lines of what the Trump administration has already attempted—including through the Alien Enemies Act of 1798. The ATRC is exactly what the executive branch-dominant process before immigration judges and the Board of Immigration Appeals is not—it’s insulated from political pressure. However the ATRC’s judges come out in individual cases, the substance and timing of the review the statute contemplates would be deeply antithetical to any attempt to use its procedures in a large number of cases at any one time. It’s a scalpel, not a bazooka.

Third, and militating in the other direction, the fact that the government had never previously used this process in the 30 years it’s been on the books speaks to the discomfort that just about everyone who’s ever looked carefully at the statute has come away with. Democratic legal systems abhor secret evidence—not just because of the grave fairness concerns it can create but because of the corrosive effects of having these kinds of decisions made out of the public eye, no matter how faithful to the relevant legal criteria they may be. The FISA process may affect a heck of a lot more people, but no one is being removed from the country based solely on a secret decision made by a FISA judge relying on secret and uncontested evidence.

Even in a world in which the five ATRC judges are doing their level best to put the government through its paces, and to look out for the interests of the non-citizen whose liberty is at issue, it is more than a little difficult to have faith in such a process—no matter what we think of the administration that’s invoking it. All the more reason, in my view, for abolition of the ATRC—or, at the very least, substantial reform—to be added to the laundry list of lower court-directed measures that will be sorely needed the next time we have a Congress that cares. Until then, here’s another envelope-pushing move by the Trump administration to which we’ll have to pay close attention, and another example of Article III district judges serving as the principal and most meaningful check to hold the executive branch accountable.

Supreme Court Trivia: The Chief Justice’s Assignment Power and the ATRC

One of the Chief Justice’s more interesting statutory authorities is the power to “assign” (a verb that has intentionally different legal implications from “appoint”) already serving Article III judges (and justices) to temporary service on other courts. The ATRC is one of four distinct courts (or panels) staffed entirely by Chief Justice assignments; the FISA Court, the FISA Court of Review, and the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation are the other three. But the Chief Justice also has the (oft-used) authority to assign active and senior district and circuit judges (and retired justices) to temporary service on other courts. (This practice is generally referred to as “sitting by designation.”)

text:
Recently rejected asylum applications from Burmese nationals were discussed during a policy seminar on Monday, July 20. The Taiwan Association for Human Rights and the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) convened the event to develop concrete recommendations for Taiwan’s immigration and labor system reform.

Experts, scholars, and public sector representatives addressed the series of problems arising from asylum seekers' inability to obtain residency and work permits on the grounds of asylum and forced overstay. Ideas such as a "temporary alien registration certificate" were suggested to improve asylum mechanisms.

In her opening remarks, NHRC member Chi Hui-jung (紀惠容) pointed out that asylum seekers may be forced to leave their home countries due to factors such as race, politics, religion, or war. She said Article 14 of the UN’s Universal Declaration of Human Rights clearly states, “Everyone has the right to seek and to enjoy in other countries asylum from persecution,” underscoring that this is not only an international human rights requirement, but also the international community’s shared commitment to human dignity. Therefore, she said, regardless of their nationality, status, or legal position, asylum seekers’ basic freedoms, safety, work, health, and dignity should be respected and protected.

title: DACA renewal costly for single moms who hid from ICE for months - The 19th News
description:
Until it came time to renew her Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) application about two months ago.
But without her work authorization, Alexa can’t find a better job or regain any stability.
“I only work and work, and I can’t do anything else because I need to recover economically.
Bri, a Minneapolis single mother who has single-handedly been running a mutual aid network for months, said about 52 people have contacted her seeking help covering their DACA fees.
“I have a lot of families, single moms, people from my community that are reaching out asking if I know who can get help,” said Bri, whose name The 19th changed for her safety.
text:
It was a frigid January morning in Minneapolis. Alexa quietly stepped outside her apartment to heat her car for her baby, who was waiting inside in her crib.

They immediately spotted her.

At the edge of the complex, the doors of a van carrying Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents swung open. They sprinted toward her.

She remembers the guns they held, and how the sight of them caused her to drop her lunchbox in the snow, turn on the spot and run as fast as she ever had back into the safety of her apartment, back to her daughter. When she shut the door, she didn’t leave again for nearly three months.

She couldn’t work. Those months drained every penny she had saved. When her own money ran out, she had no one to turn to. A year prior, her partner died in a car accident while she was eight months pregnant, leaving her with no other family in the United States. As she kept an eye on the ICE agents outside of her window, she turned to Minneapolis’ robust mutual aid networks run by volunteers who delivered groceries, formula and diapers to her door.

When ICE finally started to withdraw from the city in April, Alexa, whose name The 19th has changed to protect her privacy, finally ventured out. She started picking up odd jobs again and life returned to some sense of normalcy.

Until it came time to renew her Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) application about two months ago.

Alexa arrived alone in the United States from Honduras when she was 14 years old, which qualified her for DACA. For years, that policy has protected her from deportation and granted her permission to work. That work permit has been her lifeline over 12 years, and every two years she has faithfully renewed it.

With no savings, she had to decide between paying her rent to keep her baby and her 5-year-old housed, or paying the application fee — $555 — plus nearly $800 in attorneys fees she usually pays to ensure the application is done correctly. She chose rent.

But without her work authorization, Alexa can’t find a better job or regain any stability. She picks up any odd job that comes her way — cleaning hotel rooms, cooking and selling food — to gather up enough to renew her permit.

“I only work and work, and I can’t do anything else because I need to recover economically. I am the only one who is here with my daughter,” Alexa said in Spanish. “This is how many of us are.”

In the months since the end of ICE’s Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis, which claimed the lives of two American citizens and saw hundreds of people with no criminal background detained, the immigrant families who hid in their homes are still reeling from the long-term effects of months of employment and income loss. One of the most pressing now: Interruptions in their immigration status or delays in paperwork that have kept them stuck in a cycle of uncertainty for nearly eight months.

Bri, a Minneapolis single mother who has single-handedly been running a mutual aid network for months, said about 52 people have contacted her seeking help covering their DACA fees. Nearly all of them are single mothers like Alexa.

“I have a lot of families, single moms, people from my community that are reaching out asking if I know who can get help,” said Bri, whose name The 19th changed for her safety. “A lot of families don’t have $500 lying around right now.”

At the start of the year, Bri amassed about $250,000 in donations to help get breastmilk donations to babies whose mothers had been detained, as well as other needs. That money helped 174 families with rent assistance and other bills. But “the need is just so high right now,” Bri said, and she’s now out of funds. Across the state, demand at food shelves and the number of eviction filings are set to hit all-time highs in 2026. In Minneapolis, the city estimates that immigrant workers with limited English proficiency lost $152 million in wages from December to March alone.

Bri has started a new GoFundMe, but no funds have trickled in yet. She’s been referring people to other local organizations, but those too are running out of money and having a harder time drawing donations or volunteers.

The support that flooded into Minneapolis at the start of the year has abated, but the problems have not.

Around town, people are on certain street corners with their tools waiting for someone to drive by and give them a job. Restaurants aren’t as full. Kids aren’t out at parks as much as they used to be. Church pews go unfilled on Sundays. Recently, two people were taken by ICE out of a front yard where they were cutting grass.

Single mothers, who work at higher rates than other mothers because they rely on the income to support their children, are already more likely to be low-income, facing higher rates of food and housing insecurity. Even three months of work disruption could put them in a precarious position, at risk of losing their housing and not having enough to feed their children.

Karen Clara, the social services director at the St. Louis Park Emergency Program, a local social services agency, said the organization has been using donations that came in at the start of the year to cover rent assistance for more than 200 families, and recently more people have been asking about aid with immigration paperwork filing fees. They’ve continued offering the rent assistance as a way to open people up to use other funds to cover filing fees, she said.

But the group is down to their last $5,000.

“I’ve been having mostly a lot of conversations with people to try to troubleshoot and think about letting them know our funding is running out. ‘How are things looking? Are you able to maybe join with another family member who is in the area to save money with rent? How are jobs working?’” Clara said.

Tracy Roy, the legal director at the Immigrant Law Center of Minnesota, said part of the problem for DACA families is there is almost no way to waive the filing fees, even for those with little to no income. On top of that, those who filed at the start of the year are seeing processing times as long as eight months in some cases, Roy said.

The Trump administration was sued last month for delays in processing DACA renewal applications, which are usually fulfilled within four to eight weeks but now can take three months or more.

For the single moms who are left to raise children after a male partner is deported, which is common among the people she sees, Clara said, there is now fear of deportation.

When they come in, Clara said, she “can see the hesitancy on their faces.”

“We’re a few months out from when things have kind of calmed down, but it’s a lot of trauma that’s gonna have to be worked through,” she said. “There’s going to be long-lasting financial effects. There are families who are torn apart.”

Ensuring they can maintain their immigrant status, she said, is “priority level number one.”

Jazmin, a single mother of two girls in Minneapolis, is preparing for her DACA to lapse in September. She was fired from her job at Target at the start of the year when she stopped going to work as ICE descended on the city. She’s back at work now, but was demoted, and her last day will be September 18 unless she can renew her DACA by September 20, when it’s set to lapse. In the meantime, she’s playing catch-up on an even slimmer budget and trying to squirrel away anything she can for her DACA renewal. With attorney fees, it will cost her about $1,300.

Jazmin has renewed the application numerous times since she got DACA in 2015 — she’s been in the United States since she was 5 years old — but this is the first time it may lapse.

“All of this is a nightmare that we all hope will end soon,” said Jazmin, who The 19th is identifying only by her first name.

As a precaution, she appointed someone to care for her girls should she get deported. With no family in the United States, she selected one of her daughters’ teachers.

“I felt like a horrible mother that day, because how could I sign my kids away to a teacher? But in that moment it was for their safety,” she said. “I felt like I failed them.”

Roy said the situation for many families exemplifies how ICE operations like Metro Surge could destabilize families’ lives for years — even for those who avoided deportation.

The attacks on immigrant families “haven’t stopped just because they’ve gotten quieter,” she said. ICE is still detaining people.

For now, her organization has been able to cover immigration paperwork filing fees for all the families who have come to them asking for help — about 100 this year — and the organization does not charge any legal fees to help with applications. But there is little legal recourse for those who are in limbo waiting to receive their permits as delays continue.

And eventually, their funds, which came in through donations largely at the start of the year, will dry up.

“It is something we are talking about internally, is how we can continue to do this if we don’t have a steady stream of donations,” Roy said.

title: ICE detained me for 80 days. America's silence is no longer an option. - USA Today
description:
The conditions in the ICE jail in Indiana, where I spent 80 long days, were degrading and dehumanizing.
Aspects of my confinement were hauntingly reminiscent of my experience growing up under a brutal Israeli military occupation in the West Bank, where we became accustomed to violent, humiliating treatment at the hands of Israeli soldiers.
When I was 22, after returning from the United States to visit family in the West Bank, I was arrested again and severely tortured, psychologically abused and brought before an Israeli military tribunal.
Why is the Trump administration undermining our constitutional rights to silence criticism of a foreign country and opinions it doesn't agree with?
Silence is no longer an option, whether it's on behalf of those wrongly held by ICE or those suffering under Israel’s illegal occupation and its U.S.-backed wars abroad.
text:
On March 30, on a morning like any other in my hometown of Milwaukee, a man in plain clothes emerged from a car speeding toward me, a handgun visible at his side, and asked, "Are you Salah Sarsour?”

Within minutes, nearly a dozen cars and some 20 agents – masked, plainclothes, one flashing a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement badge – converged on me and informed me that I was under arrest.

I was sure it was a case of mistaken identity.

After all, I have been a legal permanent resident for over 30 years with a clean record here, a business owner deeply connected to my community, and a devoted father of six children and nine grandchildren, all of whom are U.S. citizens.

I was wrong.

In a brazen assault on the First Amendment and an affront to the Constitution, I believe I was targeted, arrested and detained by the Trump administration for speaking out against the ongoing atrocities Israel is committing, just as I and so many others believe that Mahmoud Khalil, Sami Hamdi, Yaacub Ira, Leqaa Kordia and others were before me.

ICE detentions like mine are an attack on the First Amendment

As a national leader supporting some of the largest and longest-standing grassroots organizations for Palestinian rights, my arrest marked a serious escalation in the Trump administration’s repression agenda. This is not just an attack against me and others working for Palestinian freedom; it is an attempt to dismantle the very values we profess as a nation.

Although a judge on June 18 ordered my release, affirming that my speech in support of Palestinian rights is constitutionally protected, my legal battle is far from over. I still face the threat of deportation.

My case is part of a broader retaliatory pattern targeting those who have worked to expose Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza. The aim is simple and should give us all pause: to have a chilling effect on constitutionally protected free speech that the government dislikes.

The conditions in the ICE jail in Indiana, where I spent 80 long days, were degrading and dehumanizing.

I was denied appropriate testing and proper nutrition needed for my Type 2 diabetes, losing at least 30 pounds while in custody.

Basic religious accommodations, like halal food and mandatory Friday congregational prayers, were not reasonably provided, and I faced disruptions to and ridicule of my obligatory dawn prayers.

The Department of Homeland Security has claimed that all people in ICE custody get three meals a day and "proper medical treatment."

Aspects of my confinement were hauntingly reminiscent of my experience growing up under a brutal Israeli military occupation in the West Bank, where we became accustomed to violent, humiliating treatment at the hands of Israeli soldiers.

As a child of 15, I was imprisoned for two years on charges that included throwing stones and was subjected to intimidation, coercive interrogation tactics and threats of rape.

When I was 22, after returning from the United States to visit family in the West Bank, I was arrested again and severely tortured, psychologically abused and brought before an Israeli military tribunal.

Eventually, like many Palestinians before me, I signed a statement in Hebrew, a language I do not understand, hoping only that the abuse would end and that I would be allowed to return to my family.

Federal immigration officials have known about and reviewed these spurious charges against me, charges I have always categorically denied, on multiple occasions. After all, Israeli military courts ‒ which have been roundly condemned by human rights groups, including Israeli ones, as unjust ‒ convict Palestinians at a rate of almost 100%, often relying on confessions extracted through torture.

Our civil liberties are being threatened. We must protect the Constitution.

Why is the Trump administration undermining our constitutional rights to silence criticism of a foreign country and opinions it doesn't agree with? The erosion of our civil liberties is the real threat facing America today.

Even the federal judge presiding over my case questioned the government’s timing in dredging up these false, decades-old Israeli military court convictions, now being weaponized because of my lawful speech. It is a move that is as transparent as it is politically calculated.

Data shows that 97% of the more than 400,000 immigrants this administration has detained have no violent criminal history, many with American spouses or children. These were some of the same individuals I spent time with when I was held in Indiana.

My faith, my family and my community’s relentless advocacy are what sustained me while I was incarcerated. Hundreds of community members from across the political and religious spectrum, including many of my longtime partners in interfaith work, submitted sworn declarations to the court on my behalf, and thousands more signed petitions and letters to Congress.

They, along with the good people of conscience across the nation, are what continue to give me hope as I continue fighting for my freedom.

For over 30 years in the United States, I have lived by my values and served my community, and I plan to continue doing so. Silence is no longer an option, whether it's on behalf of those wrongly held by ICE or those suffering under Israel’s illegal occupation and its U.S.-backed wars abroad.

I will continue to fight for our U.S. constitutional rights to be protected, not just for myself but for all communities that have been silenced.

title: 'Mega masters' hearings pack immigration court dockets. Experts say it's a strategy to deport ...
description:
Immigration lawyers call these mass proceedings “mega masters” hearings.
Deportations ‘in abstentia’ The mega masters hearings are happening amid a backlog of 3.2 million cases nationwide and 152,000 in Massachusetts.
According to Kocher’s analysis of April and May data, about 30,000 cases were completed in mega masters hearings nationwide.
“The immigration court has historically always released policy memoranda that lays out their processes and the rules,” she said.
Michele Cantara, a volunteer court observer After watching dozens of these proceedings, Cantara said about half the people summoned don’t show.
text:
In courtroom 4 of Chelmsford immigration court sat a Mexican cowboy, with wavy hair past his shoulders, a pair of gold teeth and a trucker hat in his lap. He wore a rhinestone belt buckle the size of a motorcycle license plate. His fingers were swollen and his nails caked in dirt — evidence of his work wrangling horses on a local ranch.

The man from Michoacán stood out on this recent July morning among scores of people from Central America, Brazil and Haiti summoned before an immigration judge. Like some of the others, he had an asylum hearing scheduled two years out. Then, out of the blue, came notice of a hearing just days later.

Immigration lawyers call these mass proceedings “mega masters” hearings. They say they’re increasingly common as the Trump administration seeks to reduce a massive case backlog. But advocates argue many immigrants funneled into the courts will lose the ability to have their stories heard, and that the government's ultimate goal here is to increase deportations, even for people with legitimate claims to stay in the country.

Judge Christine Olson had more than 100 people on her docket that morning, several times the typical daily caseload. She called in about a dozen people every half hour, sometimes whole families with children. It was clear many did not understand her. A Spanish interpreter, piped into the courtroom via phone, tried speaking to a Brazilian who didn’t seem to understand Spanish. Haitian Creole speakers appeared to be the largest group.

"If they don't show up, even though this is just a scheduling hearing, that's enough for a judge to issue a deportation order, which is very difficult to undo."

Jason Giannetti, an immigration attorney

Olson called them up one at a time, marked them present, then allowed them to leave pending their next hearings. The man from Michoacán went back to his job in rural Massachusetts taking care of horses, with a hearing set for the end of August.

That hearing could decide his future in the country. But for those who don’t show up to court, the stakes on this day can be even higher. Observers say they are resulting in thousands of removal orders nationwide.

“If they don't show up, even though this is just a scheduling hearing, that's enough for a judge to issue a deportation order, which is very difficult to undo,” said immigration attorney Jason Giannetti. “It seems like it's a policy, not just a problem in the system.”

Standing outside the Chelmsford courthouse after a different mega masters hearing, Giannetti said he’s never seen anything like these proceedings in his more than two decades of practicing immigration law. He said large-scale hearings were held under prior administrations, but nowhere near this scale.

Now, according to interviews with attorneys, former immigration judges and volunteer court monitors, the courts seem to be creating new complications at every step: requiring legal documents be filed in hard copy; cramming large numbers of people into hearings; and demanding people without lawyers come in person, causing some to travel to Massachusetts from around the country for the briefest of court appearances.

“The courthouses are jammed with people that are sitting on top of one another, because there's no room for everybody who's in the waiting room,” Giannetti said.

Giannetti said some of his clients aren’t even receiving notice of the hearings by mail — a federal requirement. Instead, he said, the only way to know for sure that a hearing is scheduled is to constantly check a government website.

Deportations ‘in abstentia’

The mega masters hearings are happening amid a backlog of 3.2 million cases nationwide and 152,000 in Massachusetts. Individual cases historically can take years to complete, sometimes decades. Now, the Trump administration is pushing to limit the duration in the vast majority of cases to 365 days — and just 60 days for people in custody.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche recently told members of Congress that the effort is working. Blanche said the Executive Office of Immigration Review — the arm of the Justice Department that oversees the courts — completed more than 1 million cases since President Trump took office, reducing the backlog by nearly 450,000.

An EOIR spokesperson said the immigration courts are prepared to conduct larger group-like hearings as needed. In a statement, the spokesperson said scheduling adjustments are made “to ensure cases do not languish.”

But Austin Kocher, a research fellow at American University in Washington, D.C. who’s studying the use of mega masters hearings across the country, said they are all about ramping up deportations.

“It just means a lot of people in court — very little time for immigration judges to actually consider these cases,” Kocher said. “And for the most part, it also means people are not getting adequate notice to show up on time.”

Typically in immigration court, master calendar hearings involve 20 to 30 cases and are held ahead of individual calendar hearings, in which respondents can provide evidence and argue why they should be allowed to stay in the country.

With these new mega masters hearings, Kocher said, at least 100 cases are scheduled in a single day, and the majority result in removal orders — in which a judge grants the government’s petition to deport — especially when respondents don’t appear.

According to Kocher’s analysis of April and May data, about 30,000 cases were completed in mega masters hearings nationwide. Of those, 65% were ordered removed, and 85% of those orders were made when the respondent was not present.

“ This is a strategy for generating ‘in absentia' removal orders — full stop,” Kocher said.

“These cases are really going to shape the future of each person who walks through that courtroom,” he added.

The court watchers

Even for immigration activists, it’s hard to disagree that the administration is making the courts more efficient. But Michele Cantara, who spent years consulting Fortune 500 companies on using high tech to improve systems, said efficiency shouldn’t come at the cost of due process.

“Some of the processes I see being deployed today, as a former person who used to improve processes, I'm like, ‘Well, these are pretty good,’ — if I took away any moral compass I had,” she said.

Now 66 and retired, Cantara spends her days observing immigration proceedings in Chelmsford. She’s part of a network of volunteers monitoring the courts in Chelmsford and Boston. They’re collecting data to find litigation trends and keep tabs on whether people are getting a fair shake.

Alexandra Peredo Carroll, an immigration attorney at the Mabel Center for Immigrant Justice in Boston, is helping coordinate the non-lawyer volunteers observing court proceedings. With the constant stream of changes at the courts, Peredo said the watchers’ work helps lawyers stay prepared.

“The immigration court has historically always released policy memoranda that lays out their processes and the rules,” she said. “What we're seeing now is a lot of new trends that we don't have a lot of clarity on.”

Peredo said the primary purpose of court observing is to establish accountability.

“These are public proceedings, and the public in general has a right to observe hearings to understand how the court is ruling,” she said.

"... as a former person who used to improve processes, I'm like, ‘Well, these are pretty good,’ — if I took away any moral compass I had."

Michele Cantara, a volunteer court observer

After watching dozens of these proceedings, Cantara said about half the people summoned don’t show. And for those present, the hearings are often chaotic, with children running around the courtrooms, scores of non-English speakers without lawyers and no one to interpret.

Cantara said she can see that the dysfunction has a function: “The people who get lost in the chaos can efficiently be removed.”

Asked why she does this work, Cantara remembered growing up in Chelmsford, where her mom and dad would talk about the dangers of government overreach. They taught her about the U.S. internment of more than 100,000 people of Japanese ancestry during World War II.

“My parents told me, ‘If you are a U.S. citizen, you can't stand by and let it happen again,’ ” she said. “And I can't. I can't.”

text:
In just 10 days, two people have been shot dead during Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operations, another died in the agency’s custody, and a fourth was struck and killed by a truck while fleeing from an agent. Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 53, was driving his van to work in Texas when agents stopped him and mistook him for another man they were actually seeking. Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 26-year-old Colombian, was on his way to work in Maine when ICE officers intercepted him. His last words were: “I tried to stop.” He, too, was not the person they were looking for. José Manuel Arenas, a 45-year-old Venezuelan, suffered a heart attack while being transferred between detention facilities in Georgia.

The offensive launched by the Donald Trump administration against immigrants in the United States has claimed at least 62 lives in just 18 months, 52 in detention centers and the remainder during enforcement operations, according to an Associated Press tally that also includes U.S. citizens, and has created a climate of fear in cities across a country where immigrants make up 15.4% of the population. The largest and most deeply rooted immigrant community is the Mexican one, numbering 11.1 million people. It is also the nationality that has suffered the highest number of deaths involving ICE: 17. Following the death of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum stepped up her protests, announcing that her government would turn to the U.S. courts to demand an investigation into each of those 17 deaths.

Mexico has moved from diplomatic complaints to legal action on two fronts: through the U.S. Department of Justice and through state prosecutors’ offices in the states where the deaths occurred. It has also referred the matter to the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights. The Mexican government’s decision makes it the country that has most forcefully condemned these policies, compared with others whose nationals have either been shot during arrest operations or died while being held in detention centers run by private contractors that, according to numerous human rights organizations, fail to meet even basic standards of hygiene and healthcare while detainees await deportation.

The response from Gustavo Petro’s outgoing government in Colombia to the death of the 26-year-old, whom ICE agents handcuffed after he was already lying dead on the ground, has been more restrained. In a statement, Colombia’s Justice Ministry called for a “prompt, transparent, and impartial investigation,” expressed its condemnation, and lamented the “killing” of Johan Sebastián Durán.

Petro had a major clash with Trump over the first deportation flights carrying Colombian nationals in 2025. “A migrant is not a criminal and must be treated with the dignity every human being deserves,” he said at the time, insisting that he would not allow the flights to land. In retaliation, Trump imposed 25% tariffs on Colombian imports. The crisis eased when Petro backed down and agreed to accept the flights. Now, in a post on X, he has called on Colombia’s consulate to “file a formal complaint against the ICE officer who killed Johan Sebastián Guerrero,” accompanying the message with a photo of the agent.

Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella, who is a staunch Trump ally, has said nothing. Nor has Venezuela, which has effectively become a de facto U.S. protectorate, issued any response to the death of José Manuel Arenas while in ICE custody.

In a Latin America that Trump regards as part of the United States’ sphere of influence, and where most governments are now aligned with the political right or far right, Mexico is one of the few countries attempting to push back against pressure from Washington. Whether those legal complaints will lead anywhere remains to be seen.

“Seventeen Mexicans have died, and nothing has happened, not even the slightest apology. That is serious and speaks volumes about the cruelty of this policy and the disregard for the rights and lives of detainees,” said Tonatiuh Guillén, former head of Mexico’s National Immigration Institute and a researcher at the National Autonomous University of Mexico’s (UNAM) University Program on Development Studies. In his view, “Mexico’s response has come late, but it is important.” According to Guillén, the limited reaction from other countries to the deaths of their citizens “reveals an inability to mount a meaningful challenge to U.S. policy.”

Brazil’s government under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva also protested in January 2025, at the outset of Trump’s tumultuous second term, when a deportation flight carrying 88 Brazilians arrived with passengers restrained in handcuffs, leg shackles, and waist chains. The deportees had also traveled aboard a malfunctioning aircraft with no working air conditioning, leading some to fear for their lives. Brazil denounced the treatment as “degrading,” summoned the senior U.S. diplomatic representative, and secured permission for a member of the Brazilian Embassy to oversee future departures.

The economic, security, and immigration leverage Washington exercises over Latin America shapes how each country responds when it comes to defending the rights of its citizens living abroad. The same is true of Mexico, which must tread carefully at a particularly tense moment in its relationship with its northern neighbor. President Claudia Sheinbaum’s rhetoric has focused on denouncing U.S. interference and defending Mexican sovereignty, a message she has amplified since April, when U.S. authorities sought the extradition of 10 politicians and senior officials from the state of Sinaloa over alleged ties to drug trafficking. For the first time, the list included a sitting state governor, Rubén Rocha Moya of Sheinbaum’s Morena party, who subsequently took a leave of absence from office.

Mexico’s response to the extradition requests was to demand that U.S. authorities provide sufficient evidence of the officials’ alleged links to organized crime. The dispute remains unresolved, with the DEA making statements about a “deadly connection” between the Mexican government and the cartels. Meanwhile, the United States has announced that its crucial trade agreement with Mexico and Canada will be subject to annual review, adding a new layer of uncertainty for businesses and investors.

Sheinbaum has insisted that her government’s new legal strategy is not intended to provoke “a conflict” with the United States. Last week, she said the U.S. ambassador to Mexico had been “very receptive to our concerns.” Yet Washington’s response soon suggested otherwise. On Friday, U.S. authorities returned the letters of protest that the Mexican government had submitted to privately run immigration detention centers as a preliminary step toward possible civil lawsuits. The State Department sees the letters as an effort “to dictate the actions of U.S. government personnel operating on sovereign U.S. territory,” a warning sign that Sheinbaum’s effort to defend Mexican nationals in the United States has not been well received in Washington.

Mexico already made concessions on migration policy during Trump’s first presidency to avoid tariffs, a policy that continued under Democrat Joe Biden, as the two countries forged a partnership to curb migrant flows from the south and increasingly militarized border enforcement.

Mexican immigrants in the United States, like many other foreign nationals, live with the daily fear of an encounter with ICE, detention, and deportation. That fear affects both those with legal status and those without.

““In a family, for example, sometimes the father is undocumented, but his children, who were born in the United States, are not, and that creates fear among all family members. Every day they fear going to work, picking up the children… Even going out to the store to shop is a challenge,” said Efraín Jiménez, general coordinator of the Collective of Mexican Migrant Federations and Organizations, which is active in around 30 U.S. cities.

In recent months, ICE has tried to operate with a lower profile, but it has not stopped detaining migrants using what critics describe as heavy-handed tactics, involving armed agents who are masked, unidentified, and traveling in unmarked vehicles.

“They hire them on the fly, without checking their records,” said Jiménez, who is demanding that the United States investigate the deaths and provide proper training to agents. He welcomes Sheinbaum’s initiative, “which should not be viewed as a confrontation between countries,” and urges her to “strengthen the consular network’s capacity with more staff, financial resources, and a permanent policy of support” for a migrant community that is “transgenerational and bicultural.”

The effectiveness of the criminal legal avenue that Mexico is seeking to pursue is uncertain and “will not be swift,” predicts Ariel G. Ruiz Soto, an analyst at the Migration Policy Institute in Washington. “The Department of Justice conducts independent investigations, but as part of the executive branch, the outcomes of politically sensitive cases do not usually run counter to federal agencies backed by the White House,” he explains.

The Mexican government announced that it has already begun filing complaints with prosecutors’ offices in the states where the deaths occurred, in addition to the action brought before the Department of Justice. For now, “it is doing more for its nationals than any other Latin American country. It is among the most critical and outspoken opponents of this policy, and that is important,” says Ruiz Soto.

text:
The truce, if there ever was one, is over. The apparent calm that had kept U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) out of the major headlines in recent months has given way to a fierce storm. In the space of just one week, the agency’s whip has come down hard across the United States, leaving four people dead, two of them shot by immigration agents.

Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo died after being shot by an agent in Houston on July 7. Colombian national Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was killed by gunfire from another agent in Maine on July 13. That same day, Venezuelan national Jesús Manuel Arenas Silva died while being transferred between detention centers in Georgia. And on July 14, Honduran national Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán was fatally struck by a truck while fleeing an officer in Florida.

“Why was lethal force used on Monday morning, and why did Mr. Durán Guerrero die? The family deserves answers, and the country deserves accountability. We want ICE and government officials to explain why this keeps happening in communities across the country,” said Ryan D. Fecteau, speaker of the Maine House of Representatives.

Fecteau, a Democrat, was the first person to break the news of the 26-year-old’s death. Durán Guerrero was killed when an ICE agent shot him while he was driving to work in Biddeford, a small coastal city in southern Maine. The legislator posted the news on social media, and it spread rapidly, mixing with reports that were still emerging about the death of Salgado Araujo, who had died under similar circumstances just six days earlier.

Gone was the objective publicly stated in the Senate by the new Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, when he succeeded his predecessor, Kristi Noem, last March. During his confirmation hearing to lead the department overseeing the Trump administration’s anti-immigration campaign, the former Oklahoma senator declared that his goal for the following six months was simple: “That we’re not in the lead story every single day.”

Mullin took over the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) at one of its lowest points, following the deaths of U.S. citizens Renée Good and Alex Pretti at the hands of immigration agents during protests that spread across Minneapolis in January. Those deaths sparked outrage among much of the public, including within Republican ranks. Thousands of agents had been deployed to Minnesota to carry out large-scale immigration arrests, as they did in other cities, including Los Angeles, Chicago, Charlotte and New Orleans.

In their wake, they left a trail of pain and extraordinary violence, accompanied by dramatic images of agents throwing people to the ground, beating them and forcibly separating them from their loved ones. The result was that the actions of an agency that had been unknown to most Americans just a year earlier became a major political liability

Initial support for Trump’s immigration policy, which helped him win votes in the 2024 election, fell to record lows in February and has remained there ever since. The latest Ipsos/Washington Post poll shows that nearly 60% of Americans disapprove of his handling of immigration. Other factors, including the war with Iran and the high cost of living, have pushed the president’s overall approval rating down to 30%, the same level at which he lost his reelection bid in 2020. In January 2025, his approval rating stood at 47%.

The relative calm that followed Mullin’s arrival was largely due to the changes he sought to introduce at the department. Among them was replacing the high-profile raids in streets and workplaces frequented by migrants, such as the Home Depot parking lots and car washes that Mullin’s predecessor Kristi Noem was particularly fond of targeting, with a strategy focused on pursuing specific individuals.

Incompetent agents

The change in strategy did little to alter the outcome in the cases of Durán Guerrero and Salgado Araujo. Neither man was the target the agents were searching for. One of the most persistent criticisms of ICE operations has been the lack of professionalism of officers. The roughly 10,000 field agents on staff at the start of Trump’s second term were not enough to carry out his promised mass deportation campaign. As a result, thanks to legislative funding packages and accelerated recruitment drives, the agency more than doubled its workforce in 2025, bringing it to its current number of 22,000 agents.

“The Trump administration rushed 12,000 agents onto our streets without ensuring they were fit to carry a badge and a gun — and Republicans gave this rogue agency vast power and no accountability,” Senate Democratic minority leader Chuck Schumer wrote in a post on X on Friday.

Under Noem’s leadership, ICE sought to attract recruits by offering signing bonuses of up to $50,000, announcing that college degrees were no longer required, and lowering the minimum recruitment age to 18. The agency also shortened training to between six and eight weeks, compared with the previous 72-day basic training programme.

The lack of adequate preparation has been cited as one of the reasons behind abuses committed by agents. In February, former ICE instructor Ryan Schwank submitted a complaint to Congress describing the agency’s training process as “deficient, defective and broken.”

Standard background checks have also reportedly not been carried out consistently. On Friday, it emerged that David Brouillette, the agent who killed Durán Guerrero, had suffered from serious mental health problems since childhood and had been repeatedly accused of domestic violence by his ex-wife and daughters.

Mullin announced that, from 1 July, agents would return to the previous training programme, a measure many don’t believe will be enough to address abuses committed by ICE. According to an Associated Press tally in the absence of official figures, at least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration agents since Trump began his second term.

“We have seen presidential directives about setting quotas; when there is a quota, federal agents face immense pressure to hit that magic, imaginary number and, as a result, go after anyone they believe will help them meet it,” said Fecteau. “It’s a complex problem that ranges from training to senior leadership guidance on how ICE agents should behave and perform their duties.”

The Department of Homeland Security has been quietly pushing to double the number of daily arrests, aiming for 2,000 a day. By late June, 10,000 arrests had been recorded in just five days, according to confidential documents cited by The New York Times. The White House wants more arrests because its deportation campaign has fallen short of expectations. At the start of his term, President Trump demanded the removal of one million people, but by December 2025 the figure had only just surpassed 600,000.

“The real problem is the pressure to do more arrests and do them more quickly. And when there’s relentless pressure to do more, more, more and more, agents make mistakes,” Deborah Fleischaker, ICE’s deputy director of policy during the Biden administration, said this week on CNN.

No body cameras

The DHS has consistently defended its agents in cases involving deaths, but official accounts have often conflicted with those of eyewitnesses. After the deaths of Good and Pretti, the department pledged that agents would wear body cameras while carrying out arrests. Yet this did not happen in either the Durán Guerrero case or the Salgado Araujo case.

“That is totally unacceptable,” Biddeford Mayor Liam LaFountain said in a statement last Wednesday. “In Biddeford our police officers are fully equipped with body cameras. The department’s annual budget is less than $10 million. The fact that ICE is swimming in billions of taxpayer dollars and can’t perform a basic function like properly equipping their people is a severe indictment.”

The DHS has more than enough money to provide body cameras. In June, Congress approved, without Democratic support, an additional $70 billion to finance the administration’s anti-immigration campaign, of which $38 billion was allocated to ICE.

That appropriation came on top of the $170 billion earmarked for the campaign against migrants in the budget legislation, dubbed by the president his “Big Beautiful Bill,” which was passed in July 2025. In total, an astronomical $240 billion will be spent through the end of Trump’s term attempting to achieve the largest deportation in history that he promised.

The push to increase migrant arrests has added another 4,000 detainees to ICE facilities, bringing the current population to 63,000, according to The New York Times. Detainees report inhumane conditions, including inadequate facilities, spoiled food and insufficient access to medical care. As a result, at least 22 people have died in ICE detention centers so far this year. The total is on track to surpass the 33 deaths recorded in 2025, the highest annual figure in more than two decades.

During a speech at a National Police Week memorial event in Washington, Mullin said that his agency’s personnel are “willing to pay the extra sacrifice for us to be safe, and yet, for some reason, ICE has been demonized.”

Many Americans, however, believe there has been no shortage of reasons for that.

text:
Sen. Angus King led dozens of Senate colleagues in signing a letter to the Department of Homeland Security calling for reform of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The letter, sent Monday to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, comes after two deadly shootings involving ICE officers occurred less than a week apart in Texas and Maine. Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 57, was killed July 7 in Houston, and 25-year-old Johan Sebastian Durán Guerrero was fatally shot in Biddeford July 13.

Both men were shot during traffic stops where they were not the intended targets, by federal agents who were not wearing body cameras. Neither Salgado Araujo or Guerrero had been issued a deportation order.

The letter calls for DHS to fulfill commitments to deploy and use body cameras, strengthen officer identification requirements and review enforcement protocols.

“These recent events have further compromised the credibility of DHS and fractured public trust within communities across our country,” the senators wrote in the letter. “In each case, DHS quickly issued statements asserting that officers were acting in self-defense, even before evidence of the facts surrounding the incidents had been gathered.”

King is joined by 38 senators. They are supportive of removing dangerous criminals from communities, but efforts to do so must not endanger the public, they said in the letter.

“Rather than making our communities safer, these actions endanger our citizens and seriously undermine confidence in law enforcement generally,” the senators wrote. “By no stretch could either of the victims in Texas and Maine be characterized as ‘the worst of the worst.’”

In February, DHS shut down after Democrats and the Trump administration failed to come to an agreement about ICE reforms following two fatal January shootings in Minnesota. The letter sent to Mullin on Monday morning is largely a call to reignite the Democrats’ requests, Felling said.

“In March of this year, the White House Border Czar stated that the administration would expand the use of body-worn cameras by DHS law enforcement undertaking immigration enforcements and require footage, in addition to ending roving patrols. The recent tragedies confirm that neither of these commitments were honored,” the senators wrote.

The letter also urges immediate changes to agency branding, including exclusive and explicit identification of personnel as “ICE.” The senators request that agents cease wearing tactical gear, vests or other uniforms labeled “POLICE” or “POLICE ICE.”

Senators ended the statement by demanding detailed responses to questions regarding DHS’s plans to respond to the public, immediate changes to traffic stop and training protocol and additional oversight to ensure public safety.

text:
A group of 44 migrant support, refugee and human rights organisations have called on the Government to urgently close large-scale asylum accommodation sites at former military bases, describing the conditions are inhumane and warning that people are being denied access to legal support and advice.

In an eight-page letter to the Home Secretary (available here), the groups criticised the use of sites in Crowborough, East Sussex, and Wethersfield, Essex to house asylum seekers, as well as planned new sites in Bicester, Barnham, and Linton-on-Ouse.

The letter was co-ordinated by the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants (JCWI) and follows visits by legal representatives and support organisations to residents at Crowborough and ongoing work by charities supporting people at both sites. It says asylum seekers, many of whom will have experienced multiple traumatic events, are being housed in poor, unhygienic, prison-like conditions. Living conditions at Crowborough are described as freezing during winter months and excessively hot during summer heatwaves.

Highlighting what it calls "inhumane" conditions at the East Sussex site, the letter continues: "[R]esidents are being housed in communal rooms with as many as 16 to a room. This is unsafe, undignified and morally wrong. It also appears to contradict a recent High Court ruling that the changes to Home Office policy removing the protective presumption that survivors of torture, trafficking or other forms of serious physical, psychological or sexual violence and those with disabilities should not be forced to share rooms was unlawful."

The organisations said they also believed the Home Office is failing its statutory duties under the Modern Slavery Act 2015 by not properly screening arrivals to identify victims of trafficking. Most of the residents at Crowborough that said they were victims of trafficking told JCWI's lawyers that the Home Office did not ask them about this and the questions they did ask did not encourage or allow them to self-identify.

A lack of access to legal advice is another central concern. The organisations say that people held in the former military sites do not have access to justice, with substantive asylum interviews are being conducted while residents are effectively cut off from legal support. Residents at Crowborough are said to be attending interviews without ever having spoken to a lawyer or received proper legal advice.

The letter explains: "At Crowborough, as continues to be the case at Wethersfield, this access is being systematically obstructed, due to both camps being situated in legal aid deserts, as well as lack of communication infrastructure and delayed correspondence. … Official correspondence to the camp is often severely delayed or sent to email addresses the men do not know how to access. This lack of communication means that men are missing critical deadlines for their legal cases. We were told of cases of delays in post receipt leading to missed tribunal deadlines, potentially deciding their fate without them having a fair chance to present their case."

The organisations also criticised the cost of large-scale accommodation sites, stating that housing asylum seekers in former military facilities was more expensive than community-based accommodation. They cited a cost of £135 per night at Wethersfield compared with £23.25 per night for dispersal accommodation, according to figures from the National Audit Office referenced in their letter.

Griff Ferris, spokesperson for JCWI, called on the Government to close the "shameful camps", describing the treatment of asylum seekers as "disgustingly cruel and inhumane". Charlotte Khan of Care4Calais said the sites were harmful to refugees' health and wellbeing and re-traumatising for survivors of torture and modern slavery.

Sophie McCann of Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) UK commented: "MSF medical teams have witnessed first-hand the severe psychological harm caused by these mass containment sites, particularly for people have already survived torture, persecution, violence and detention. These performatively cruel policies must end. People seeking safety must be housed in dignified accommodation with communities."

description:
The FBI will no longer participate in investigations into cases involving alleged assaults on immigration agents, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.
The federal law enforcement agency would instead be deferring such investigations to Homeland Security Investigations, the sources said.
HSI is an arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, both of which are overseen by the Department of Homeland Security, meaning the immigration enforcement agency would effectively be investigating incidents involving its own agents.
The Department of Homeland Security denied that changes were in store in a social media post on Sunday.
